ai_director_pacing.problem: Hand-authored enemy/item placement makes a level deterministic: players memorise every encounter, derive one optimal strategy and the experience degrades into a race. Conversely, constant unmoderated combat is fatiguing and long quiet stretches are boring. The method adds a runtime controller that estimates each player's 'emotional intensity' and modulates the threat population to produce peaks and valleys of tension, while procedurally populating the world to keep replays unpredictable.

implementation_variants.name: Intensity-driven phase machine (Build Up / Sustain Peak / Peak Fade / Relax)
implementation_variants.description: Per-survivor intensity scalar increases on damage, incapacitation, ledge-pull and nearby infected deaths (inversely proportional to distance), and decays towards zero over time except while infected are actively engaging. The controller tracks the max intensity across the team and drives four phases: Build Up (full threat population), Sustain Peak (continue full population 3-5 s after peak), Peak Fade (switch to minimal population but wait for a natural break in the action), Relax (minimal population for 30-45 s, or until the team has travelled far enough toward the next safe room).

implementation_variants.name: Structured unpredictability (superposition of randomised population functions)
implementation_variants.description: Population is generated by superposing several population functions whose space and/or time parameters are randomised within designer-defined ranges (e.g. mob spawns at a randomised interval of 90-180 s, at a randomised spot behind the survivor team). The result is neither purely random nor deterministically uniform.

implementation_variants.name: Active Area Set (AAS) spawn/recycle with flow distance and potential visibility
implementation_variants.description: The navmesh is preprocessed with a flow distance (travel distance from the start safe room to each area) and potentially-visible area sets. The AAS is the set of nav areas surrounding the player team; the director creates population as areas enter the AAS and deletes it as they leave, allowing hundreds of enemies to be represented using a small set of reused entities. Spawn location filters use flow distance (behind / ahead / near a specific entity / anywhere) and invisibility to the team.

implementation_variants.name: Hard-capped category budgets (expert-derived variant)
implementation_variants.description: Independent of an intensity curve, each population category (wanderers, specials, bosses, pickups) is given a hard concurrent cap and a minimum respawn interval so that worst-case CPU/AI cost is bounded even if the intensity estimator misbehaves. L4D additionally exempts boss encounters from adaptive pacing because removing them distorted overall pacing too much.

ai_director_pacing.applicability_conditions: Replayable session-based games where the same maps are played many times (co-op survival, horde/arena, roguelite). Requires a spatial representation (navmesh or area graph) over which flow distance and visibility can be precomputed, plus a pool of reusable NPC entities. Not applicable to tightly authored narrative set-pieces where encounter composition must be exact.
ai_director_pacing.limitations: Tuning is qualitative and playtest-driven; there is no published way to derive the intensity thresholds analytically. The intensity model is an estimate of player emotion, not a measurement, so it can mis-fire on players who take damage deliberately. Boss-tier content is typically excluded from pacing control (documented in L4D). Procedural population interacts with every downstream system (navlinks, audio propagation, AI visibility), so it must be integrated with those systems rather than bolted on. Determinism/reproducibility is harder if randomised per session.
ai_director_pacing.required_data_and_tools: Navmesh or area graph with per-area flow distance and potentially-visible sets; entity pooling system; per-category spawn tables; a debug HUD/telemetry overlay showing phase, intensity per player, and active population counts; replay/seed recording for A/B comparison.

impact.cpu: low-medium (per-frame intensity aggregation + periodic spawn decisions over a bounded area set; no published measurement)
impact.gpu: none
impact.ram: low-medium (preallocated NPC pools + per-area population counts; L4D stores wanderers as a simple count N per area rather than live entities)
impact.network: low (in co-op the director is server-authoritative; only spawn/despawn events replicate, and recycling keeps the entity churn low)

ai_director_pacing.quality_impact: High positive on perceived variety and replayability: the game session is read as a skill challenge rather than a memorisation exercise. Risk: visible popping if the AAS boundary is inside the camera frustum, and perceived unfairness if spawns happen in view.
ai_director_pacing.concept_impact: Significant. It converts encounter design from 'place N enemies here' to 'define population functions and an intensity model', and it makes replayability a systems property rather than a content-volume property.

behaviour_tree_update_budget.problem: Behaviour trees (and equivalent HFSM/action systems) are cheap per tick but are evaluated for every agent every frame. At high agent counts the aggregate cost becomes a frame budget problem, and uniform ticking wastes work on agents that are far away, off-screen or behaviourally static. The method decouples decision frequency from render frequency so that total AI cost is bounded and predictable.

implementation_variants.name: Event/action encapsulated behaviour split with explicit update ownership
implementation_variants.description: L4D splits each actor into Locomotion / Body / Vision / Intention subsystems; Intention owns a system of concurrent behaviours (HFSM + stack) built from Actions with OnStart/Update/OnEnd/OnSuspend/OnResume and atomic transitions (Continue / ChangeTo / SuspendFor / Done). Events propagate innermost-child-first, then to buried actions, then to the parent. Because decisions are atomic transition results, behaviour work can be skipped or deferred without corrupting state.

implementation_variants.name: Significance-driven tick rate (engine-provided framework)
implementation_variants.description: Unreal's Significance Manager provides a central framework that evaluates each registered object's significance against one or more view transforms and lets project code throttle work: 'running complex AI code less frequently', shutting off particle emitters, or enacting a per-Actor-type budget so that only a limited number of AI pawns run at high detail when many cluster near the camera. Epic documents explicitly that the manager itself does not improve performance - the savings come from the project's own response to significance values.

implementation_variants.name: Fixed per-frame agent budgets / round-robin tick groups
implementation_variants.description: A hard cap on the number of agents that may re-evaluate their tree in a frame, with the remainder carried to the next frame (round-robin). Combined with distance/significance tiers this bounds worst-case AI cost. This is the general industry shape; the specific numbers are project-specific and are expert_estimate here.

implementation_variants.name: Data-oriented batch evaluation (see ecs_data_oriented_crowd)
implementation_variants.description: Rather than throttling individual trees, restructure the decision logic as a data-oriented processor over component arrays so that all agents of a class are evaluated in one cache-friendly pass, making the per-agent overhead small enough that throttling becomes an optimisation rather than a requirement.

behaviour_tree_update_budget.applicability_conditions: Any game with more than a few dozen concurrently thinking agents, or with expensive perception/decision logic per agent. Requires that agents tolerate a reaction latency of one to a few frames (combat-critical agents are usually exempted and ticked every frame). Works best where the agent set can be partitioned into significance tiers (player-adjacent, on-screen, off-screen, dormant).
behaviour_tree_update_budget.limitations: Throttling adds reaction latency, which is directly visible in combat responsiveness; critical agents must be exempt, which reintroduces unbounded cost under clustering. Significance/post-significance callbacks run in parallel in Unreal and therefore must be thread-safe (or registered as Sequential, which loses the parallelism). Skipping ticks can starve time-dependent logic (timers, cooldowns) if those are driven by tick rather than by absolute time. Epic documents that the framework provides no benefit by itself.
behaviour_tree_update_budget.required_data_and_tools: A CPU profiler with per-agent/per-subsystem instrumentation; a significance or distance metric; a debug overlay showing each agent's tier, last-tick time and reaction latency; a stress scene with a known agent count.

behaviour_tree_update_budget.concept_impact: Low. This is an engineering-scaling method, not a design change, provided the exempted (player-facing) agents keep full fidelity.

npc_perception_budget.problem: Perception (line-of-sight, field-of-view, hearing, 'can I see X' queries) is usually the most expensive per-agent AI subsystem because it touches the physics/nav world. Evaluating it for every agent against every candidate every frame scales poorly and produces frame spikes when agents cluster. The method bounds perception cost by budgeting queries, caching recognised sets and reusing shared spatial data.

implementation_variants.name: Dedicated Vision subsystem owning LOS/FOV and a recognised-entity set
implementation_variants.description: L4D gives each actor a Vision component that owns line-of-sight, field of view and 'am I able to see <X>' queries, and that maintains the actor's recognised set of entities. Perception therefore has a single owner that can be budgeted, and downstream behaviours consume a cached set rather than issuing ad-hoc queries.

implementation_variants.name: Navmesh-derived visibility queries (flow distance + potentially visible areas)
implementation_variants.description: Rather than raycasting against the render world, precompute potentially-visible area sets over the navmesh and answer 'has area A ever been seen by actor B' / 'is area X potentially visible by area Y' as area-graph queries. L4D uses the navmesh for exactly this class of spatially-localised question, including for the director's 'where is a spot near the Survivors, not visible to any of them' query.

implementation_variants.name: Significance-tiered perception rate
implementation_variants.description: Perception query rate is driven by the same significance value used for behaviour ticking: nearby/on-screen agents query every frame or every other frame, distant agents query every N frames. Unreal's Significance Manager is the documented framework for supplying that value.

implementation_variants.name: Shared/stimulus-side perception (inverted query)
implementation_variants.description: Instead of every agent scanning for targets, sources emit stimuli (sound events, muzzle flashes) into a spatial structure and agents consume the nearby stimuli. This inverts the cost from O(agents x candidates) to O(agents + stimuli). This variant is expert_estimate in this pack - no verified primary source was found for a specific shipped implementation.

npc_perception_budget.applicability_conditions: Games with more than a handful of agents that must react to the player or to each other. Requires either a physics/world query API with raycasts or a precomputed visibility structure over the navigation/area graph. Most valuable when agents cluster, which is exactly when naive perception blows the frame budget.
npc_perception_budget.limitations: Budgeting perception adds detection latency, which players perceive as 'the AI is dumb' or 'the AI is cheating' depending on direction. Cached recognised sets can go stale if the world changes (e.g. a wall is destroyed) unless the change invalidates them - Rainbow Six Siege documents that destruction changes AI visibility through partially broken walls and that destruction listeners must be asynchronous. Raycast-based perception is only as good as the collision representation, which may differ from the visual representation. Navmesh-derived visibility costs memory and precompute time.
npc_perception_budget.required_data_and_tools: Physics/nav query API (raycasts or area visibility), a spatial index for candidate selection, CPU profiler instrumentation per query type, debug rendering of FOV cones and query rays, a recorded stress scenario.

npc_perception_budget.concept_impact: Low to medium. Perception latency is a direct gameplay parameter (stealth games treat it as a core mechanic), so budgeting it is partly a design decision.

flow_field_pathing.problem: Per-agent A* over long paths is O(agents x path length) and must be rebuilt whenever an agent is pushed off its path by another unit, terrain, or an explosion. In large battles the rebuilt path causes a second and third collision, and the simulation grinds to a halt; the usual mitigation (forcing units to stay on their original path) then cripples physics, formations and hit reactions. Flow fields move the cost from per-agent pathfinding to a per-tile field that every agent in that tile can share.

implementation_variants.name: Cost / integration / flow field triad over a sector grid with portals
implementation_variants.description: Supreme Commander 2 divides the world into sectors of 10x10 grid squares connected by portals. Three fields per sector: a cost field (prebuilt by the editor from walls and slope, with 50-70% of pathable space marked 'clear'), an integration field (24-bit: 16 bits integrated cost + 8 bits flags such as 'active wave front' and 'line of sight'; optionally 40-bit using a 32-bit float for better results) and a flow field (8-bit: 4 bits direction index + 4 bits flags such as 'pathable' and 'has line of sight').

implementation_variants.name: Merging A* over the portal graph + per-portal flow field requests
implementation_variants.description: A path request first runs A* through the portal node graph, then runs 'merging' A* for subsequent sources so walkers prefer to stop at an already-traversed portal node. Each next-portal node in the result submits a flow field request. Because only the portal graph is searched, the request uses very little CPU.

implementation_variants.name: Flow field cache with reference tracking and prebuilt permutations
implementation_variants.description: Built flow fields are stored in a cache keyed by a unique ID based on the portal window they take you through, so work is shared across path requests with different goals (a two-way hallway yields the same field). Fields are reference-tracked and can be discarded or put on a discard timer; all permutations can be prebuilt and stored on disk so only custom line-of-sight goal information needs building at runtime.

implementation_variants.name: Dirty-marking + priority rebuild queue with fixed millisecond time slices
implementation_variants.description: Moving goals rebuild only the goal's flow field (most other fields are already cached). Changing walls and hills mark the containing sector's cost field and its portals dirty; the portal graph and affected paths are rebuilt via a priority queue where each item gets a time slice of a fixed number of milliseconds, giving explicit control over what rebuilds when.

flow_field_pathing.applicability_conditions: Large numbers of agents (hundreds to thousands) moving to a small number of shared goals over a large map - RTS, large-scale battles, horde crowds. Assumes a grid or grid-like world representation and that agents can steer locally (agents read a direction and blend it as they cross grid squares). Less useful for a few agents with highly individual long paths, where per-agent A* is simpler and cheaper.
flow_field_pathing.limitations: Every agent in a tile shares one direction field, so per-agent preferences (terrain cost by unit class, personal avoidance) need extra handling - the chapter handles this with separate movement-type paths ('most restrictive movement type' first). Memory: an integration field per active goal per sector (24-bit or 40-bit per cell) plus an 8-bit flow field. Dynamic geometry forces field rebuilds, which must be time-sliced or they cause spikes. The chapter recommends against integrating over all eight neighbours (costly) and instead uses a cheap line-of-sight pass to avoid diamond-shaped flow near the goal. 3D spaces were listed as future work, not shipped.
flow_field_pathing.required_data_and_tools: A grid/sector world representation with portal connectivity; an editor that can bake cost fields from walls and slope and visualise them; a flow field cache with reference tracking; a time-sliced rebuild queue; debug visualisation of cost/integration/flow fields and of the portal graph.

impact.cpu: high reduction vs per-agent A* at high agent counts (replaces repeated per-agent path rebuilds with shared per-tile work); the chapter reports 'very little CPU' for the portal-graph request phase and uses a fixed-ms time slice for rebuilds, but gives no absolute benchmark
impact.gpu: none (CPU-side in the described implementation; a GPU variant is possible but not described in this source)
impact.ram: medium (integration field 24-bit/cell or 40-bit/cell plus 8-bit flow field per cached sector-goal combination; mitigated by the cache, reference tracking and on-disk prebuilt permutations)
impact.disk: low-medium if flow field permutations are prebuilt and streamed from disk (listed in the chapter, partly as future work)
impact.network: none directly (in a lockstep RTS all clients must build identical fields)

flow_field_pathing.quality_impact: Positive: agents move instantly with no path rebuild stall, so they respond immediately to player commands, and physics/formations/hit reactions become possible because being pushed off-path no longer forces a repath. Neutral on path optimality: the result is 'reasonably close to optimized' rather than optimal.
flow_field_pathing.concept_impact: Medium-high. Enables game scenarios that were impossible with fixed-path movement: explosions that push units around, super-large robots pushing a hundred tanks, whirlwind structures that suck units across the map.

effort_person_days.formula: p50 = 4 (sector/portal graph) + 4 (integrator: cost + LOS + flow passes) + 3 (flow field cache + reference tracking) + 2 (dirty-marking + time-sliced rebuild queue) + 2 (debug field visualisation) = 15; p80 = p50 x 2.0 (integration-field edge cases - LOS corners, overlapping wave fronts, movement types - are the main source of rework) = 30. Assumes an existing grid world; excludes converting a polygon navmesh world to a grid.

navmesh_tiling_streaming.problem: A single monolithic navigation mesh cannot fit in memory for a large or open world, cannot be rebuilt incrementally when the world changes, and cannot be loaded/unloaded per region. Tiling the navmesh and streaming tiles enables large/dynamic environments, local rebaking, and hierarchical planning.

implementation_variants.name: Tiled Recast navmesh + Detour runtime queries
implementation_variants.description: Recast rasterises input triangles into voxels, filters un-walkable voxels, divides the walkable areas into polygonal regions and re-triangulates them into a navmesh. It can build a single navmesh (simple, static cases) or a tiled navmesh (larger, more dynamic environments). Tiled meshes enable re-baking, hierarchical path-planning and navmesh data-streaming. Recast is dependency-free C++98 under the ZLib license and powers AI navigation in Unity, Unreal, Godot and O3DE.

implementation_variants.name: DetourTileCache for streaming and dynamic obstacles
implementation_variants.description: The DetourTileCache module is described specifically as 'Navmesh streaming. Useful for large levels and open-world games', separate from Detour (runtime loading, pathfinding, queries) and DetourCrowd (agent movement, collision avoidance, crowd simulation). An automated fetch of a guessed deep doc page returned 404, so no parameter-level claim is made about tile size or compression.

implementation_variants.name: Hierarchical planning over the tile/portal graph
implementation_variants.description: Search at a coarse level (tile or portal graph) then refine within a tile. Recast lists hierarchical path-planning as an advanced Detour feature enabled by tiled meshes; the flow-field chapter implements the analogous coarse level as a portal node graph searched with merging A*.

implementation_variants.name: Rebaking dirty tiles at runtime (destruction / dynamic geometry)
implementation_variants.description: Tiled meshes allow only affected tiles to be re-baked when geometry changes. Rainbow Six Siege documents the gameplay-side requirement: navlinks must be updated when floors/walls become breached or trapdoors open.

navmesh_tiling_streaming.applicability_conditions: Open-world or large-level games, or any game with runtime geometry changes (destruction, buildable structures, moving platforms). Requires a navmesh generation pipeline integrated into the editor/build and a runtime that can load/unload tiles. Overkill for small, static, single-level games where a solo mesh is simpler.
navmesh_tiling_streaming.limitations: Recast's own docs state tiled meshes are 'more complex to work with' than single meshes. Tile boundaries introduce seams that need correct link generation; agents crossing a boundary need the adjacent tile resident or they stall. Streaming introduces latency - a tile must be built/loaded before an agent needs it. Rebaking costs CPU and must be time-sliced. Memory is proportional to resident tiles, so a high draw-distance world still needs many tiles resident.
navmesh_tiling_streaming.required_data_and_tools: Recast/Detour (or an equivalent navmesh SDK), an editor integration that bakes and names tiles, a streaming/IO layer for tile load/unload, a debug drawer for the navmesh and tile boundaries, and a profiler marker around bake and load operations.

impact.cpu: low-medium steady state (tile load + link fixup); medium-high spike during a rebake unless time-sliced
impact.gpu: none
impact.ram: medium-low vs a monolithic mesh (only resident tiles); scales with the number of tiles kept resident
impact.disk: medium (baked tile data on disk; size scales with world size and navigation resolution)
impact.network: none (server-side only; but destruction-driven nav changes must replicate their effect on AI)

navmesh_tiling_streaming.quality_impact: Enabling rather than degrading: it is what makes navigation possible at all in a large or mutable world. Risk of visible failures (agents stalling at unloaded tile boundaries, or failing to path through a freshly opened breach).
navmesh_tiling_streaming.concept_impact: Medium. It is a precondition for open-world and destructible-environment designs; without it, world size and mutability are capped by navigation memory.

effort_person_days.formula: p50 = 3 (integrate Recast/Detour or equivalent) + 2 (bake pipeline + tile naming/versioning) + 3 (streaming load/unload + boundary link fixup) + 2 (runtime rebake path, time-sliced) + 2 (debug draw + stress test) = 12; p80 = p50 x 2.2 (tile-boundary and streaming-latency bugs are the dominant rework source) = 26.4 -> 26. Assumes the engine already exposes navigation; excludes authoring navmesh generation parameters from scratch.

dependencies: A navmesh generation pipeline (Recast or engine equivalent)
Streaming/IO infrastructure for tiles

relations.note: Tiled polygon navmesh + per-agent A* vs grid flow fields; different world representations and different agent-count sweet spots.
Both bound navigation cost per frame; tiling bounds memory and rebake scope, time-slicing bounds query cost.
Destruction requires navmesh rebake; R6 Siege documents navlink updates for trapdoors and breachable walls.

navmesh_tiling_streaming.verification: Measure: (a) peak resident navmesh memory on a scripted traversal of the world (should stay flat, not grow monotonically), (b) time to build one tile (p50/p99) and the max frame time during a scripted burst of tile loads, (c) correctness: run 1000 agents across tile boundaries and assert zero agents permanently stuck at a boundary, (d) after a scripted destruction event, assert navlinks are updated within the configured rebake window and that an agent can path through the new opening.

claims.statement: Recast documentation states single navmeshes are suitable for many simple, static cases and are easy to work with, while tiled navmeshes are more complex to work with but better support larger, more dynamic environments.
claims.locator: Section 'How it Works' - 'Single meshes are suitable for many simple, static cases... Tiled navmeshes are more complex to work with but better support larger, more dynamic environments.'

claims.statement: Tiled Recast meshes enable advanced Detour features: re-baking, hierarchical path-planning, and navmesh data-streaming.
claims.locator: Section 'How it Works' - 'Tiled meshes enable advance Detour features like re-baking, heirarchical path-planning, and navmesh data-streaming.'

claims.statement: DetourTileCache is documented as the module for 'Navmesh streaming. Useful for large levels and open-world games', distinct from Detour (pathfinding/queries) and DetourCrowd (crowd simulation and collision avoidance).
claims.locator: Module list - 'DetourTileCache/ - Navmesh streaming. Useful for large levels and open-world games'

claims.statement: Recast powers AI navigation features in Unity, Unreal, Godot, O3DE and 'countless AAA and indie games and engines'; it is licensed under the ZLib license and requires only a C++98-compliant compiler.
claims.locator: Features list - 'Recast powers AI navigation features in Unity, Unreal, Godot, O3DE and countless AAA and indie games and engines'; License section

claims.statement: Recast builds a navmesh in four steps: rasterise input triangles into voxels; filter/remove voxels where agents cannot move; divide the walkable voxel areas into polygonal regions; re-triangulate those regions into a navmesh.
Rainbow Six Siege documents that AI navigation requires navlink updates for trapdoors, breachable walls and floors.
claims.locator: PDF p.25, 'AI Navigation: Navlink Update - Trapdoors, Breachable Walls, Floors'

game_examples.fact: Procedural destruction is integrated with AI navigation: the game updates navlinks for trapdoors, breachable walls and floors as the environment changes.
game_examples.non_transferable: Confirms the requirement (nav must follow destruction), not a tiling or streaming implementation. R6 Siege is a small-map multiplayer game, so its navigation footprint is not comparable to an open world; no memory or bake-time figure transfers.

game_examples.fact: Uses A* through a navigation mesh and additionally uses the navmesh for flow distance (travel distance from the start safe room to each area) and potentially-visible area sets - i.e. the navmesh is a spatial reasoning structure, not just a pathfinding one.
game_examples.non_transferable: L4D uses linear campaign maps; there is no evidence in the source of tiled streaming. The transferable idea is navmesh-as-spatial-index, not the streaming mechanism.

rvo_local_avoidance.problem: Global pathfinding tells an agent which way to go but not how to avoid the other agents going the other way. Naive avoidance produces oscillations, reciprocal dancing, and agents stopping dead. RVO/ORCA formulates local avoidance as reciprocal collision avoidance: each agent takes half the responsibility for avoiding a pairwise collision, and the optimal action is found by solving a low-dimensional linear program per agent.

implementation_variants.name: ORCA (Optimal Reciprocal Collision Avoidance) - half-plane constraints + linear program
implementation_variants.description: Each agent independently senses its neighbours and computes a collision-free velocity by solving a low-dimensional linear program over ORCA half-planes; each agent takes half of the responsibility for each pairwise avoidance. The authors prove the resulting motions are smooth and report computing collision-free actions for thousands of agents in dense 2D/3D scenarios 'in only a few milliseconds'.

implementation_variants.name: RVO2 open-source library (OpenMP-parallelised)
implementation_variants.description: RVO2 is an open-source (Apache 2.0 since 2016-05-04) C++ implementation with a simple API: the user supplies static obstacles, agents and preferred velocities, then steps the simulation. It exploits multiple processors via OpenMP. RVO2-3D is the 3D variant without static obstacles. Third-party Python bindings exist.

implementation_variants.name: Neighbour-capped, spatially-hashed local avoidance
implementation_variants.description: In a shipped game the neighbour set is typically capped (K nearest neighbours within a radius) and sourced from a spatial hash or the crowd system's own grid so per-agent cost is bounded regardless of local density. This is the standard shape of the integration and is expert_estimate here - the RVO2 page does not document a neighbour cap.

implementation_variants.name: Engine-integrated crowd avoidance (DetourCrowd / Unreal Mass Avoidance)
implementation_variants.description: Rather than a standalone library, use the engine's crowd module: Recast's DetourCrowd provides 'agent movement, collision avoidance, and crowd simulation'; Unreal's Mass Avoidance is 'a force-based avoidance system integrated with MassEntity'.

rvo_local_avoidance.applicability_conditions: Any scene with more than a few agents moving in shared space: crowds, RTS squads, co-op NPC companions, sports/vehicle AI. Assumes agents are reasonably modelled as velocity-controlled discs/cylinders and that a preferred velocity is available from the global planner. Most effective in 2D/2.5D; full 3D (RVO2-3D) exists but is less commonly used and, in the RVO2-3D variant, does not handle static obstacles.
rvo_local_avoidance.limitations: ORCA assumes reciprocal (cooperative) avoidance; it does not model agents with differing priorities unless you bias the responsibility split, so a 'player pushes through crowd' behaviour needs extra work. The guarantee is collision-free given that neighbours are also avoiding - it degrades when some agents do not participate (e.g. the player). Dense, high-pressure crowds can still jam; the ORCA page's own numbers are offline simulation, not a game frametime. Cost scales with neighbour count, so a neighbour cap is required in practice. Static obstacle handling differs between the 2D and 3D library variants.
rvo_local_avoidance.required_data_and_tools: RVO2/RVO2-3D or an engine crowd module (DetourCrowd, Unreal Mass Avoidance); a preferred-velocity source (pathfinder or flow field); a spatial hash/grid for neighbour queries; a debug renderer for velocity obstacles and chosen velocities; a soak scenario with agents crossing in opposite directions.

impact.cpu: low-medium (per agent per frame: neighbour query + small LP); the ORCA authors report collision-free actions for thousands of agents 'in only a few milliseconds' in their simulation testbed - offline, not a shipped-game frametime
impact.gpu: none in the reference implementation (ClearPath, a related parallel GPU formulation, exists but was not the basis of a claim here)
impact.ram: low (position/velocity/preferred-velocity arrays plus a neighbour buffer)
impact.network: none directly; in multiplayer, local avoidance is usually client-authoritative and non-deterministic, which conflicts with lockstep determinism

rvo_local_avoidance.quality_impact: High positive on movement believability: removes the reciprocal dancing and 'agents stop and stare at each other' artefacts of naive steering. Also removes the need for the global planner to repath on every contact.
rvo_local_avoidance.concept_impact: Medium-high: enables dense crowds and formation movement as a designed feature rather than a source of bugs; also enables the physics-based gameplay scenarios (explosions pushing units, large units shoving crowds) that fixed-path movement forbids.

effort_person_days.formula: p50 = 2 (integrate RVO2 or engine crowd module) + 2 (preferred-velocity plumbing from the existing pathfinder) + 2 (neighbour cap + spatial hash) + 2 (priority/asymmetry handling for player and special agents) + 2 (debug draw + soak test) = 10; p80 = p50 x 2.0 (jam/deadlock and player-priority edge cases dominate rework) = 20. Excludes writing the solver from scratch.

dependencies: A global path source (navmesh A* or flow fields) providing preferred velocities
A spatial index for neighbour queries

relations.note: Flow fields supply global direction, RVO/ORCA supplies local separation; the flow field chapter explicitly relies on physics/steering once agents can move in any direction.
DetourCrowd in the Recast family provides agent movement and collision avoidance alongside tiled navmesh queries.

Local avoidance is typically non-deterministic and client-authoritative; using it in a deterministic lockstep title creates divergence risk. A fixed physics/simulation timestep is a prerequisite for determinism but does not by itself make avoidance deterministic.

rvo_local_avoidance.verification: Two soak tests: (a) opposing flow - two groups of N agents cross a corridor in opposite directions for 10 minutes; assert zero overlapping-agent frames beyond a small penetration tolerance and zero permanently stuck agents; (b) density ramp - increase agent count until the frame budget is hit and record the agent count at which p99 avoidance time exceeds budget. Also measure mean detour length vs the unobstructed path to confirm avoidance is not over-steering.

claims.statement: ORCA lets each agent take half the responsibility for avoiding pairwise collisions and reduces selecting the optimal action to solving a low-dimensional linear program; the authors prove the resulting motions are smooth.
The authors report testing ORCA on dense, complex simulation scenarios in 2D and 3D involving thousands of agents and computing collision-free actions for all of them 'in only a few milliseconds'.
claims.locator: 'Description' section - 'involving thousands of agents, and compute collision-free actions for all of them in only a few milliseconds'

claims.statement: The published ORCA demonstration videos include a crowd simulation with 25,000 agents in a virtual Hajj scenario, and a 3D case with 812 agents on a sphere moving to antipodal positions.
RVO2 Library and RVO2-3D Library became open-source software on 2016-05-04 under the Apache License, Version 2.0; the latest listed versions are RVO2 v2.0.2 and RVO2-3D v1.0.1.
The RVO2 library exploits multiple processors when available using OpenMP for parallelisation of the simulation.
RVO2 Library has been licensed for the video game Warhammer 40,000: Space Marine from developer Relic.
Unreal provides Mass Avoidance, described as a force-based avoidance system integrated with MassEntity; Recast provides DetourCrowd for agent movement, collision avoidance and crowd simulation.
claims.locator: MassEntity child page list; and SRC-AIS-011 module list

game_examples.fact: The RVO2 Library maintainers state the library 'has been licensed for the video game Warhammer 40,000: Space Marine from developer Relic', and quote a Daily Telegraph review noting that with many orks on screen 'the framerate never takes a hit'.
game_examples.non_transferable: Confirms the library was licensed for a shipped title, but not which agent counts or subsystems used it, nor the integration cost. The newspaper quote is a review impression, not a measurement, and does not transfer as a performance number.

game_examples.fact: Agents push each other and slide along walls using physics rather than a reciprocal-avoidance solver; this enabled explosions that push units back and super-large robots that push back a hundred tanks.
game_examples.non_transferable: This is the physics-based alternative to RVO/ORCA, not an ORCA implementation. The specific gameplay scenarios (whirlwind structures, robots pushing a hundred tanks) depend on that game's physics integration and unit mass model; no avoidance cost or agent count transfers.

time_sliced_pathfinding.problem: A single A* query over a large navmesh can take several milliseconds. If many agents request paths on the same frame (spawn wave, goal change, destruction event), the queries stack into a multi-frame stall. Time-slicing splits a query across frames so no single frame exceeds its pathfinding budget.

implementation_variants.name: Detour sliced query API (initSlicedFindPath / updateSlicedFindPath / finalizeSlicedFindPath)
implementation_variants.description: Detour exposes an explicit sliced pathfinding workflow: call initSlicedFindPath() to initialise the sliced query, call updateSlicedFindPath(maxIter, &doneIters) repeatedly until complete, then finalizeSlicedFindPath() to retrieve the path. finalizeSlicedFindPathPartial() returns a partial path when the search has not finished, letting an agent start moving along a partial result. maxIter is the caller's per-frame iteration budget.

implementation_variants.name: Global per-frame query budget with a priority queue
implementation_variants.description: Requests go into a priority queue (by agent significance, distance or request age) and a scheduler spends a fixed iteration or millisecond budget per frame across the queue. The flow field chapter uses the same shape for rebuilds: 'each item in the queue is given a time slice of a fixed number of milliseconds'.

implementation_variants.name: Hierarchical / coarse-to-fine search
implementation_variants.description: Search a coarse graph first (portals or tile graph) and refine locally, which reduces the work that needs slicing at all. Recast lists hierarchical path-planning as a tiled-mesh feature; the flow field chapter uses a portal node graph with merging A* so that 'you've only traversed the portal node graph using merging A*, you've used very little CPU'.

implementation_variants.name: Job-system / worker-thread pathfinding
implementation_variants.description: Offload whole queries (rather than slices) to worker threads using the engine's job system, so the game thread only pays the handoff. This is the alternative to slicing and is what Unity's C# Job System exposes; the Unity page could not be content-extracted in this pass so no numeric claim is made from it.

time_sliced_pathfinding.applicability_conditions: Games where many agents can request paths in the same frame, or where a single query is long relative to the frame budget (large maps, high navmesh resolution). Requires the pathfinder to be resumable (an explicit sliced API or a coroutine/job). Less necessary when agent counts are low and queries are short.
time_sliced_pathfinding.limitations: Slicing adds latency between request and result; agents must handle 'no path yet' (usually by standing still, continuing on the old path, or following a partial path). State must be preserved per pending query, which costs memory and complicates cancellation when an agent dies or its goal changes. If the request rate exceeds the budget, the queue grows unboundedly, so a cap or drop policy is required. finalizeSlicedFindPathPartial gives a partial path, which may be worse than waiting.
time_sliced_pathfinding.required_data_and_tools: A resumable pathfinding API (Detour's sliced API or equivalent), a request queue with priorities, per-frame budget configuration, a profiler marker on the pathfinding phase, and a stress scene that issues a burst of N simultaneous requests.

impact.cpu: medium-high reduction in worst-case (p99/max) pathfinding frame time; total CPU work is unchanged or slightly higher (queue overhead)
impact.gpu: none
impact.ram: low (one search state per pending query; bounded by the queue cap)
impact.network: none

time_sliced_pathfinding.quality_impact: Positive on smoothness (no pathfinding-driven frame spikes). Risk of visible latency: an agent may take several frames to start moving after a command, which players perceive as unresponsiveness if the budget is too small.
time_sliced_pathfinding.concept_impact: Low. Purely an engineering-smoothness method; it should be invisible to design.

effort_person_days.formula: p50 = 1 (adopt resumable API / wrap existing query) + 1.5 (priority queue + per-frame budget) + 1 (partial-path and cancellation handling) + 1.5 (burst stress test + profiler markers) = 5; p80 = p50 x 2.2 = 11. Assume the pathfinder already exists; this excludes writing a resumable A* from scratch (add ~8 d to p50).

dependencies: A resumable pathfinding API (Detour sliced queries) or a job system
A navmesh (see navmesh_tiling_streaming)

relations.note: Tiling bounds memory and rebake scope; slicing bounds query cost per frame. Both are needed for large/dynamic worlds.
Sharing one flow field across many agents removes the per-agent query entirely, which can make slicing unnecessary for crowd-scale movement.
Moving queries to worker threads is the alternative to slicing them within a frame; the two can also be combined.

time_sliced_pathfinding.verification: Issue a burst of N=500 simultaneous path requests on one frame, with slicing on vs off. Measure max frame time and p99 frame time over the following 60 frames, plus the distribution of request-to-result latency. Acceptance example: max pathfinding time per frame stays under the configured budget (e.g. 1 ms) in both configurations' p99 comparison, and p95 request latency stays below the design responsiveness window. Also assert the pending queue drains (no unbounded growth) over a 5-minute soak with a continuous request stream.

claims.statement: Detour exposes a sliced pathfinding API: initSlicedFindPath() to initialise, updateSlicedFindPath(const int maxIter, int* doneIters) to advance under a caller-supplied iteration budget, and finalizeSlicedFindPath() to retrieve the result.
Detour provides finalizeSlicedFindPathPartial(), which returns the best partial path found when the sliced search has not yet completed.
The per-frame budget is expressed as a maximum iteration count (maxIter) passed to updateSlicedFindPath, with the number of actually-completed iterations returned via doneIters.

In the flow field system, dynamic rebuilds are handled by marking data dirty and rebuilding via a priority queue where each item receives a time slice of a fixed number of milliseconds - the same budget-control pattern applied to rebuilds rather than queries.
Recast documents hierarchical path-planning as an advanced feature enabled by tiled navmeshes, offering a way to reduce per-query work rather than spread it over frames.
No published measurement of the frame-time improvement from time-sliced pathfinding was found in this pass.

game_examples.fact: Uses the analogous budget pattern for dynamic rebuilds: data is marked dirty and rebuilt through a priority queue where each item gets a fixed-millisecond time slice, controlling what, when and how rebuilding happens over time.
game_examples.non_transferable: This is time-slicing applied to flow-field rebuilds, not to per-agent A* queries. The specific millisecond slice value is not published, and the pattern's benefit depends on that game's rebuild volume; no frame-time number transfers.

agent_update_budget.problem: When hundreds or thousands of NPCs are alive, updating all of them every frame (behaviour, perception, movement, animation) exceeds the CPU budget. The method assigns each agent a significance value and distributes a fixed per-frame update budget across agents, so the total cost is bounded and the highest-value agents (near the camera, in combat, player-controlled) get the most frequent and most detailed updates.

implementation_variants.name: Centralised significance evaluation framework (Unreal Significance Manager)
implementation_variants.description: A single USignificanceManager evaluates registered objects against one or more view transforms using project-supplied FSignificanceFunction callbacks, then invokes FPostSignificanceFunction callbacks (Concurrent, run in parallel and thread-safe; or Sequential, run in sorted order). Project code reacts by disabling components, lowering tick rates, or - as an advanced use - grouping similar actors and enacting a per-Actor-type budget so that only a limited number of AI pawns run at high detail when many cluster near the camera.

implementation_variants.name: Hard AI-count budget with LOD swap (Assassin's Creed Unity 'AI Recycling')
implementation_variants.description: Ubisoft's GDC talk describes a pooling system that swaps low-res NPCs for high-res NPCs without the player noticing, plus a 'simplistic AI brain' to animate thousands of NPCs. The stated limits are 40 real AIs and 120 high-resolution models, which together supported a scene with 10,000 crowd NPCs on screen simultaneously.

implementation_variants.name: Distance/visibility-tiered update rates
implementation_variants.description: Agents are bucketed into tiers (e.g. full / reduced / minimal / dormant). Each tier has its own tick interval and feature set (full: perception + behaviour + animation; minimal: position integration only). This is the general industry shape and is expert_estimate here.

implementation_variants.name: Data-oriented parallel update over all agents
implementation_variants.description: Instead of throttling, restructure agent update as a parallel data-oriented pass (Unity DOTS / Unreal MassEntity) so the per-agent overhead falls enough to update everyone every frame; Unity documents IXION using ECS for 'heavy NPC simulation'.

agent_update_budget.applicability_conditions: Games with tens-to-thousands of simultaneous NPCs, especially where they cluster (market scenes, crowds, RTS). Requires that most agents are fungible: the player cannot track individual distant NPCs closely enough to notice reduced fidelity. Requires a cheap significance metric (distance to view, screen coverage, combat state).
agent_update_budget.limitations: The framework does not itself save anything - every saving comes from project code responding to significance (explicitly documented by Epic). Significance and post-significance callbacks run in parallel and must be thread-safe unless registered Sequential. Reduced update rates cause visible artefacts when an agent crosses tiers (animation popping, delayed reactions) unless transitions are smoothed or hidden by the pooling/swap technique. Hard caps (40 real AIs) mean the majority of NPCs cannot have genuine individual behaviour, which constrains design: any NPC the player must meaningfully interact with has to be inside the cap.
agent_update_budget.required_data_and_tools: A significance framework or a hand-rolled tier system; an entity pool for low/high-detail swapping; per-tier feature flags; a CPU profiler with per-tier aggregation; a debug overlay showing each agent's tier and last update time; a stress scene at 2x the design maximum agent count.

impact.cpu: high reduction in AI/agent update time at scale (mechanism documented; magnitude project-specific)
impact.gpu: low-medium reduction if the swap also reduces animation/skinning and draw detail (see crowd_instancing_impostors)
impact.ram: low-medium (agent pools for both detail levels; the alternative - full-detail state for every agent - is worse)
impact.vram: low-medium (depends on whether the low/high swap changes mesh/animation residency)
impact.network: low-medium reduction in replicated actor updates if network relevancy is driven by the same significance value

agent_update_budget.quality_impact: Neutral to positive when the swap is hidden (AC Unity's explicit goal was swapping 'without the player noticing'). Negative if tier transitions are visible or if an NPC the player is watching is demoted.
agent_update_budget.concept_impact: Medium. It forces an explicit decision about how many NPCs are 'real' versus set dressing, which is a design constraint, not just an optimisation.

effort_person_days.formula: p50 = 2 (significance metric + registration) + 2 (tier table + per-tier feature flags) + 2 (budget enforcement / round-robin scheduler) + 2 (debug overlay + stress scene) = 8; p80 = p50 x 2.2 = 17.6 -> 18. Excludes an entity-pool LOD-swap system (see crowd_instancing_impostors, +6 d p50) and excludes an ECS rewrite.

dependencies: A significance/distance metric
Optional: an entity pool with low/high detail variants (see particle_pooling for the pattern)

relations.note: Update budgeting bounds CPU; instancing/impostors bound GPU. Both are needed for thousands of NPCs.
Behaviour-tree tick throttling is the decision-logic slice of the same budget.
Restructuring to a data-oriented framework can remove the need for a budget by making per-agent update cheap.

agent_update_budget.verification: Stress scene at 2x the design maximum agent count, 10-minute soak. Measure p50/p95/p99 agent-update CPU time per frame, per-tier agent counts over time, and the number of tier transitions per second. Acceptance: p99 update time stays under the allocated budget and does not grow over the soak; and a scripted camera flythrough shows zero visible tier pops in a recorded capture reviewed frame-by-frame (or, if pops exist, they occur outside the player's attention cone).

claims.statement: Epic documents that the Significance Manager itself does not improve performance; it is an extensible framework whose Update() is called by the project (typically once per frame) and whose benefit comes from project-defined responses.
claims.locator: 'The Significance Manager itself does not actually improve performance'; 'The Update function does not run automatically. In most cases, developers will want to call it every frame, and only once per frame.'

claims.statement: A documented advanced use is grouping similar actors and enacting a per-Actor-type budget, e.g. limiting how many AI-controlled pawns run at high detail when several players are clustered near the camera.

Assassin's Creed Unity shipped a scene with 10,000 crowd NPCs on screen at the same time using a limit of 40 real AIs and 120 high-resolution models, swapping low-res for high-res NPCs via a pooling system intended to be unnoticeable.
The stated real-AI limit in the Assassin's Creed Unity crowd system is 40 concurrent genuinely-simulated AIs, with 120 high-resolution NPC models.
claims.locator: GDC Vault session overview - 'With the limit of 40 real AIs and 120 high resolution models'

claims.statement: Unity documents Kasedo Games using ECS for Unity 'to power heavy NPC simulation' for IXION, as an alternative to throttling.

game_examples.fact: Ships a crowd system with AI level-of-detail and pooling that swaps low-res NPCs to high-res ones; with a cap of 40 real AIs and 120 high-res models the team reports a scene with 10,000 crowd NPCs on screen simultaneously.
game_examples.non_transferable: 10,000 on-screen NPCs with 40 real AIs is that game's crowd budget for a Paris street scene on PS4/Xbox One. It is not a performance number and does not transfer: the acceptable ratio of 'real' to 'fake' NPCs depends entirely on how closely the camera can inspect them, which is a design property. No frame time is published.

game_examples.fact: IO Interactive's GDC talk describes the techniques and optimisations used to achieve 1200-character crowds in a real production level while running at 30 fps on current-gen consoles, with every character individually interactable and influenceable.
game_examples.non_transferable: '1200 characters at 30fps on current-gen consoles' is a 2012 PS3/Xbox 360 target for that game's specific crowd density and camera. Neither the agent count nor the frame rate transfers to other hardware or to a different crowd/interaction design. The talk also states the requirement was that players can interact with and influence each individual character - a design constraint that drives the cost.

crowd_2d_instancing.problem: In a 2D (or 2.5D) game, drawing hundreds or thousands of crowd agents as individual sprites/quads produces one draw call (or one dynamic batch) per agent and per layer, and saturates the CPU render thread long before the GPU is busy. Batching all agents of a class into a single instanced draw removes the per-agent draw overhead.

implementation_variants.name: Single instanced draw per crowd class
implementation_variants.description: All agents sharing a sprite and material are drawn in one instanced draw call with per-instance transform, colour and animation-frame data supplied via an instance buffer. Unity documents GPU instancing for this purpose (page not content-extractable in this pass).

implementation_variants.name: Data-oriented batch with an ECS/DOTS framework
implementation_variants.description: Store agent transforms in contiguous component arrays and have a single system write the instance buffer, so the CPU cost is one linear pass instead of per-object traversal. Unity DOTS is documented as being used for gameplay logic at scale; Door 407 report DOTS being 'especially useful for pathfinding and optimizing our gameplay logic' in an RTS.

implementation_variants.name: Impostor flipbook instancing (animated 2D crowd)
implementation_variants.description: Per-agent animation is a flipbook frame index rather than a skeletal animation; the frame index rides in the instance data so a single draw renders agents at different animation phases. This is the 2D analogue of 3D impostor crowds and is expert_estimate here.

implementation_variants.name: Engine particle system as a crowd renderer
implementation_variants.description: Treat crowd agents as GPU-simulated particles with a sprite renderer, which gives batching and simulation in one system. Unreal's Niagara documentation notes GPU sims allow a greater number of particles and describes consolidating emitters and using spawn-index groups for variation.

crowd_2d_instancing.applicability_conditions: 2D/2.5D games with large numbers of visually similar agents (crowd backgrounds, RTS units, bullet-hell entities, sports spectators). Requires that agents share a material and that per-agent variation can be expressed as instance data (transform, UV flipbook frame, tint). Least useful when every agent needs a unique material or a unique mesh.
crowd_2d_instancing.limitations: Per-agent state must fit the instance buffer layout; changing the layout later is invasive. Sorting/transparency is a problem: instanced draws cannot easily be depth-sorted per instance, which matters for 2D games that rely on draw order. Per-instance animation is limited to frame indices or shader-driven motion unless you skin on the GPU. If the crowd needs real animation variety, the number of distinct flipbooks (and therefore draws) grows.
crowd_2d_instancing.required_data_and_tools: An instancing-capable renderer (Unity GPU instancing, engine equivalent), a sprite atlas or flipbook texture set, an instance buffer writer, and a frame capture/profiler to count draw calls and measure render-thread time.

impact.cpu: medium-high reduction in render-thread/CPU time (draw call count drops from O(agents) to O(distinct agent classes)); no published measurement found in this pass
impact.gpu: low (more vertices/instances per draw, but far better batching; typically GPU-bound only at very high instance counts)
impact.ram: low (instance buffer sized to max agents; smaller than per-agent game objects)
impact.network: none

crowd_2d_instancing.quality_impact: Neutral to positive: allows far denser crowds than would otherwise be possible. Risk: uniformity (all agents looking identical) unless variation is baked into the atlas and frame selection.
crowd_2d_instancing.concept_impact: Medium: dense crowds become affordable, which changes what a 2D scene can depict (a packed stadium or street rather than a handful of characters).

effort_person_days.formula: p50 = 1 (instance buffer + writer for one agent class) + 1 (atlas/flipbook authoring pipeline) + 1.5 x 2 (two variation channels: tint, animation frame) + 0.5 (draw-call verification capture) = 5; p80 = p50 x 2.4 (transparency/draw-order and per-class material splits are the usual surprises) = 12. Assumes the engine already supports instancing.

dependencies: An instancing-capable renderer
A sprite atlas / flipbook set (see flipbook_particles, sprite_particle_atlas)

relations.note: Same batching idea; crowd_2d_instancing is the sprite/quad case, crowd_instancing_impostors is the 3D mesh/impostor case.
Data-oriented storage makes writing the instance buffer a single linear pass.
Flipbook frame index as per-instance data is the shared mechanism for cheap per-agent animation.

crowd_2d_instancing.verification: Capture a frame with the crowd at maximum density. Count draw calls and set-pass/state changes for the crowd (before: approximately one per agent; after: one per agent class). Measure render-thread CPU time and GPU time for the crowd pass. Acceptance example: draw calls for the crowd reduced by >90% and render-thread time for the crowd under the allocated budget, with no visual regression in a before/after screenshot diff at 1080p.

claims.statement: Unity documents GPU instancing as a rendering path for drawing many copies of the same mesh/material in fewer draw calls; the manual page was confirmed live but its body could not be extracted in this pass, so no Unity-specific limit or number is claimed.
claims.locator: Page resolves; body behind cookie-consent interstitial

claims.statement: Unity reports Door 407 using DOTS 'almost everywhere' in their RTS Diplomacy is Not an Option, 'especially useful for pathfinding and optimizing our gameplay logic'.

Epic's Niagara best-practice documentation states GPU simulations 'in most cases ... are more performant, and allow for a greater number of particles' than CPU simulations, though it warns that a 1-particle simulation 'can potentially take up the same resources as one with 64 particles'.

No published measurement of draw-call or CPU savings from 2D crowd instancing was found in this pass; the directional claim is derived from the mechanism (O(agents) draws -> O(classes) draws), not measured.

game_examples.fact: Unity documents that the studio uses DOTS 'almost everywhere' in this real-time strategy game and finds it 'especially useful for pathfinding and optimizing our gameplay logic' - the data-oriented foundation that makes large-unit-count 2D/RTS crowd rendering tractable.
game_examples.non_transferable: This is a vendor marketing page quoting the developer. It confirms DOTS usage for gameplay/pathfinding, not specifically 2D crowd instancing, and gives no unit counts or frametime numbers.

crowd_instancing_impostors.problem: Thousands of 3D crowd NPCs cannot each be a unique animated skinned mesh: the draw call count, skinning cost and animation evaluation cost all scale with the crowd size. Instancing renders many copies of a shared mesh in one draw; impostors replace distant NPCs with cheap camera-facing representations (billboards, cards, or pre-baked animation textures) so that the full-detail path is reserved for the few NPCs the camera can actually inspect.

implementation_variants.name: Pooled LOD swap between low-res and high-res NPC representations
implementation_variants.description: Assassin's Creed Unity's 'AI Recycling' talk describes a pooling system that swaps low-res NPCs for high-res NPCs without the player noticing, allowing thousands of replicated, persistent, interactive NPCs with hard limits of 40 real AIs and 120 high-resolution models.

implementation_variants.name: Data-oriented mass entity rendering (Unreal MassEntity / Mass Avoidance)
implementation_variants.description: Unreal's MassEntity is 'a gameplay-focused framework for data-oriented calculations' with an integrated Mass Avoidance force-based system; this is the engine-supported path to representing and moving very large NPC sets without per-actor overhead.

implementation_variants.name: Impostor/billboard LOD for distant crowd members
implementation_variants.description: Distant agents are rendered as camera-facing impostors (optionally with pre-baked animation flipbooks), reserving skinned meshes for near agents. The mechanism is the crowd analogue of the hair-card technique Epic documents as the traditional real-time approximation for hair.

implementation_variants.name: Instanced skinned animation via animation-texture baking
implementation_variants.description: Skinning is pre-baked into a texture sampled per instance, so many agents can show different animation phases in a single instanced draw. This is expert_estimate here - no verified primary source was found in this pass.

crowd_instancing_impostors.applicability_conditions: Crowds of hundreds to tens of thousands where the camera cannot inspect every individual (street scenes, stadiums, battlefields, RTS armies). Requires a significance/distance metric to drive the LOD swap, a pool of both representations, and - ideally - a data-oriented agent representation. Not applicable when every NPC must be unique and close-up inspectable.
crowd_instancing_impostors.limitations: The LOD swap is only free if it is unnoticeable; that is a hard art/animation problem, not a solved one, and depends on camera framing. Impostors break down at silhouettes and under close inspection, and they do not cast correct shadows. Hard caps on real AIs mean most NPCs are decorative; any designed interaction must be inside the cap. Instanced animation via baked textures costs VRAM and limits animation blending. Epic's groom docs note the equivalent trade-off for hair: strands need 'an allocated performance budget and is not supported on all platforms', with cards as the fallback - the same shape of constraint.
crowd_instancing_impostors.required_data_and_tools: An instancing-capable renderer; an impostor/billboard generator or artist-authored impostors; an entity pool; a significance metric (see agent_update_budget); a frame capture tool to count draw calls; a profiler measuring render-thread and GPU time for the crowd pass.

impact.cpu: high reduction in draw-call submission and animation/skinning cost at crowd scale (mechanism documented; magnitude project-specific)
impact.gpu: medium reduction (fewer draws and far less vertex/skinning work; adds impostor overdraw at distance)
impact.ram: medium (two representations resident in pools; data-oriented storage is more compact than per-actor objects)
impact.vram: low-medium (impostor atlases and/or baked animation textures; one shared mesh set rather than per-NPC meshes)
impact.network: none directly

crowd_instancing_impostors.quality_impact: Enabling: makes dense crowds possible at all. Risk: visible popping at the swap distance, uniform-looking crowds, and incorrect shadows from impostors.
crowd_instancing_impostors.concept_impact: High. Dense believable crowds change what scenes a game can stage (a living city rather than an empty one), but the hard caps force designers to treat 'who is a real NPC' as a scarce resource.

effort_person_days.formula: p50 = 3 (instancing path + instance buffer) + 3 (impostor generation or authoring) + 3 (LOD swap / pooling integration with the significance metric) + 1.5 (shadow handling for impostors) + 1.5 (frame-capture verification) = 12; p80 = p50 x 2.2 (the 'must not be noticeable' requirement drives long art/animation iteration) = 26.4 -> 26. Excludes an ECS/MassEntity restructure.

dependencies: A significance/distance metric (see agent_update_budget)
An entity pool (see particle_pooling)
Optional but strongly complementary: ecs_data_oriented_crowd

relations.note: The same significance value should drive both update frequency and render LOD so CPU and GPU budgets stay aligned.
Data-oriented agent storage is what makes writing instance buffers cheap at crowd scale.
Same batching principle applied to sprite quads rather than 3D meshes/impostors.
Both replace expensive per-element geometry (strands / skinned meshes) with card approximations at distance; Epic documents cards as the traditional real-time fallback.

crowd_instancing_impostors.verification: Frame capture at maximum crowd density: count draw calls and set-pass calls for the crowd (target: one per class/LOD, not per agent); measure render-thread and GPU time for the crowd pass. Then run a scripted camera doll-in from impostor distance to full-detail distance on a single NPC and review the recorded capture frame-by-frame for a visible pop. Acceptance example: zero detectable pops across 20 sampled NPCs, and crowd draw calls under a fixed cap regardless of agent count.

claims.statement: Assassin's Creed Unity achieved a scene with 10,000 crowd NPCs on screen at the same time with a limit of 40 real AIs and 120 high-resolution models, using a pooling system to swap low-res and high-res NPCs unnoticeably.

Hitman: Absolution shipped 1200-character crowds in a production level at 30 fps on current-gen (2012) consoles, with the stated requirement that players can interact with and influence each individual character.

Unreal's MassEntity is documented as a gameplay-focused framework for data-oriented calculations, with Mass Avoidance as an integrated force-based avoidance system - the engine's supported path for large agent sets.
claims.locator: MassEntity index page and child page list

claims.statement: Epic documents the same budget/fallback shape for hair: strand geometry 'needs an allocated performance budget and is not supported on all platforms', and grooms can rely on cards or meshes when strands are not possible.
No published draw-call or GPU-time measurement for 3D crowd instancing/impostors was found in this pass; the impact bands above are derived from the mechanism, not measured.

game_examples.fact: Ships AI level-of-detail with a pooling system that swaps low-res NPCs to high-res NPCs; the reported result is 10,000 crowd NPCs on screen at once under limits of 40 real AIs and 120 high-res models.
game_examples.non_transferable: The 10,000 / 40 / 120 numbers are a single scene's budget on 2014 consoles for a game whose camera is usually above and away from the crowd. They do not transfer as capacity figures: the binding constraint is how close the camera can get to an individual NPC, which is a design choice. No frame time or draw-call count is published.

game_examples.fact: Ships 1200-character crowds at 30 fps on PS3/Xbox 360 with the requirement that players can interact with and influence each individual character; IO Interactive presented the techniques and trade-offs at GDC.
game_examples.non_transferable: 1200 characters at 30fps is a 2012 console target for a fixed third-person camera and a specific crowd density. Neither number transfers to modern hardware or other designs. The interactability requirement, not the count, is the transferable constraint.

ecs_data_oriented_crowd.problem: Object-oriented per-actor agent code (virtual dispatch, pointer-chasing, per-actor allocation) wastes most of its time on memory traffic and bookkeeping rather than on the actual simulation. At crowd scale this overhead, not the algorithm, is the bottleneck. A data-oriented ECS stores agent state in contiguous component arrays and runs systems as linear passes, making the per-agent cost small and parallelisable.

implementation_variants.name: Unity ECS for Unity + Burst + C# Job System (DOTS)
implementation_variants.description: Unity's DOTS combines ECS (data-oriented framework, 'enabling seasoned Unity creators to achieve more thanks to an unprecedented level of control and determinism'), the Burst compiler (IL/.NET bytecode to optimised native code via LLVM, with CPU intrinsics) and the C# Job System (safe parallel code on multi-core).

implementation_variants.name: Unreal MassEntity / MassGameplay
implementation_variants.description: Unreal's MassEntity is 'a gameplay-focused framework for data-oriented calculations', with Mass Avoidance (force-based avoidance), MassGameplay, a Mass Debugger and a simplified Mass Processor/Query API (Query Executor).

implementation_variants.name: Component decomposition with explicit update ordering
implementation_variants.description: Nystrom's Component pattern states the intent as 'Allow a single entity to span multiple domains without coupling the domains to each other', slicing a monolithic entity into domain components. The documented caveats are exactly the ECS risks: component communication becomes harder (shared state vs direct references vs messaging) and update order becomes an implicit, bug-prone dependency.

implementation_variants.name: Actor-subsystem decomposition without full ECS
implementation_variants.description: A middle path: keep actors but split them into domain subsystems with explicit update phases and explicit event propagation. L4D ships this: Locomotion / Body / Vision / Intention, with events propagating innermost-child-first, then to buried actions, then to parent, and atomic action transitions (Continue/ChangeTo/SuspendFor/Done).

ecs_data_oriented_crowd.applicability_conditions: Games with thousands of homogeneous entities that all need the same processing (crowds, projectiles, RTS units, swarms), or codebases where feature count is growing faster than the team can manage complexity. Requires discipline: components must be plain data, and systems must declare what they read/write. Much less valuable for a handful of bespoke, heterogeneous entities.
ecs_data_oriented_crowd.limitations: ECS is an architectural commitment, not a drop-in optimisation: retrofitting an existing actor-based game is expensive. The documented caveats of decomposition apply with full force - communication between components and, critically, implicit ordering dependencies ('we would wrongly render Bjorn at his position on the last frame'). Debuggability suffers (no single object to inspect). ECS does not help when the bottleneck is the algorithm or the GPU. Vendor performance quotes are marketing: the only number Unity publishes on the DOTS page is a single studio's anecdote ('processes that initially took an hour now take only 100 milliseconds'), not a benchmark.
ecs_data_oriented_crowd.required_data_and_tools: An ECS framework (Unity Entities/ECS, Unreal Mass, EnTT, or in-house), a job/task system, a profiler that can show per-system time and cache misses, an entity debugger (Unity's ECS debugger or Unreal's Mass Debugger), and a synthetic benchmark that scales entity count.

impact.cpu: high reduction in per-entity CPU overhead and much better parallel scaling when applied to homogeneous crowds (mechanism documented; the only published figure found is a vendor-quoted anecdote, not a benchmark)
impact.gpu: none directly (enables the instancing path in crowd_instancing_impostors)
impact.ram: medium reduction vs per-actor objects (contiguous typed arrays, no per-object headers/vtables); increases if archetype fragmentation is uncontrolled
impact.network: low-medium improvement if determinism is exploited for rollback/replay networking

ecs_data_oriented_crowd.quality_impact: Neutral directly. Indirectly positive: the freed CPU budget goes into more agents or better behaviour. Indirectly negative if the decomposition is done badly and ordering bugs appear.
ecs_data_oriented_crowd.concept_impact: Medium. Determinism and cheap scale enable designs (huge crowds, replay/rollback, deterministic QA) that are impractical with per-actor OO code. But it constrains how gameplay code is written for the whole project.

effort_person_days.formula: p50 = 6 (archetype/component design + core systems) + 2 x 3 (three agent systems ported: movement, avoidance, behaviour) + 4 (job/task integration + scheduling and ordering) + 4 (debugging tooling, entity inspector, benchmarks) = 20; p80 = p50 x 2.25 = 45 (retrofitting existing gameplay and chasing ordering bugs dominates; ranges up to a full project rewrite). Use only when the project is greenfield on the agent systems, or the agent count is a core design pillar.

dependencies: An ECS framework or the decision to build one
A job/task system for parallelism

relations.note: ECS removes the per-agent overhead that makes budgeting necessary; budgeting is the cheaper, non-architectural response.
Both rely on a job system and on declaring read/write access for safe parallelism.
ECS is the extreme form of composition; the Component pattern's caveats (communication, ordering) apply to both.
ECS makes the CPU side cheap; instancing makes the GPU side cheap. Both are needed for a 10k crowd.

ecs_data_oriented_crowd.verification: Build a synthetic benchmark with N entities (sweep N from 1k to 10x the design target) doing a representative mix of movement, avoidance and decision work. Compare the ECS implementation against the existing actor-based implementation on the same hardware: measure p50/p99 frame time, per-system CPU time, and - if available - cache-miss counters. Acceptance example: near-linear scaling in N up to the design target and p99 frame time under budget at 2x the target. Also assert determinism: run the same inputs twice and compare a hash of entity state - it must match (this is what makes the ECS path valuable for networking/QA).

claims.statement: Unity's DOTS is documented as comprising ECS for Unity ('a data-oriented framework compatible with GameObjects, enabling ... an unprecedented level of control and determinism'), the Burst compiler (IL/.NET to optimised native code via LLVM, exposing CPU intrinsics) and the C# Job System (safe parallel code on multi-core).
claims.locator: 'ECS for Unity', 'Burst Compiler', 'C# Job System' sections

claims.statement: Unity quotes Blackbird Interactive on Hardspace: Shipbreaker: 'We had processes that initially took an hour now take only 100 milliseconds after implementing DOTS.' This is a single studio's anecdote on a vendor marketing page, not a benchmark.

Nystrom's Component pattern documents that splitting an entity into components makes the system implicitly dependent on update order, and getting the order wrong produces 'subtle, hard-to-track bugs' such as rendering an entity at the previous frame's position.
claims.locator: Section 'How do the components communicate?' / ordering discussion

claims.statement: Nystrom documents three component communication options with distinct costs: modifying shared container state (decoupled but implicit and memory-wasteful), referring directly to each other (simple and fast but tightly coupled), and messaging via the container (fully decoupled but most complex).

Left 4 Dead ships a non-ECS decomposition into Locomotion / Body / Vision / Intention with event propagation innermost-child-first, then buried actions, then parent, and atomic action transitions - a lighter-weight way to get domain separation.
Unreal's MassEntity is documented as 'a gameplay-focused framework for data-oriented calculations' with Mass Avoidance as an integrated force-based avoidance system.

game_examples.fact: Unity documents that Stunlock Studios used ECS throughout the development of V Rising, an open-world multiplayer survival game, including world building in the Editor with custom visual scripting and scalable open-world streaming.
game_examples.non_transferable: Vendor production page. Confirms full-project ECS adoption in a shipped multiplayer survival game, but reports no entity counts, no frametime, and no evidence about crowd-specific use. Adoption by one studio is not evidence that ECS is the right choice for a different team's codebase maturity.

game_examples.fact: Blizzard's GDC 2017 talk states Overwatch uses an Entity Component System architecture, and that the team 'leverages ECS to curtail complexity, even as they continue to add new crazy features'; the same talk covers how the networked simulation uses determinism for responsiveness and precision.
game_examples.non_transferable: Confirms ECS shipped in a hero shooter, but Overwatch's entity count is small (dozens of actors) - the motivation there was complexity management and determinism for netcode, not crowd scale. That motivation does not transfer to a project whose problem is thousands of homogeneous agents.

game_examples.fact: Unity documents that Kasedo Games used ECS for Unity 'to power heavy NPC simulation' for IXION, a city-builder/survival/space-exploration title - the closest documented match to a crowd-scale ECS workload in this pack.
game_examples.non_transferable: Vendor page, no numbers. 'Heavy NPC simulation' is not quantified, so no agent count or frametime transfers.

cloth_baked_animation.problem: Real-time cloth simulation costs CPU/GPU per simulated character and is unstable under fast motion, teleports and camera cuts. For background characters, cinematic-only moments, and LODs beyond a certain distance, cloth motion can be pre-authored (baked into animation, or baked to a vertex-animation texture) and played back with zero simulation cost.

implementation_variants.name: Cloth motion baked into the skeletal animation
implementation_variants.description: The cloth is authored as part of the character's animation (or as extra skinned bones driven by the animation) so it is evaluated by the existing animation/skinning path with no solver. This is the standard background-character approach and is expert_estimate here.

implementation_variants.name: Max-distance / backstop limited simulation as a safety net
implementation_variants.description: Unreal's Chaos Cloth 'Masks' document the parameters that exist precisely to constrain simulation back toward authored motion: 'Max Distance is the maximum distance any point on the cloth can move from its animated position', Backstop Distance offsets that limit, Backstop Radius prevents movement into a sphere, and Anim Drive Multiplier 'drive[s] springs that pull clothing towards its animated position' - explicitly noted as a control for animators in cinematics or animation-driven scenes. Baking is the limit case where the drive is total.

implementation_variants.name: Imported cloth/geometry cache playback (Alembic-style)
implementation_variants.description: Offline-simulated cloth is imported as a per-frame geometry cache and played back; Epic's groom documentation notes an equivalent exists for hair (imported Groom Caches). This is a documented pattern for hair and is expert_estimate as applied to cloth in this pack.

implementation_variants.name: LOD-driven switch from simulation to baked
implementation_variants.description: Near characters simulate; distant ones play baked motion. The parameters documented for Unreal cloth painting make the authored-motion fallback explicit: paint value 0 means 'the skinned vertex could not move' (fully baked) and 100 allows one metre of movement.

cloth_baked_animation.applicability_conditions: Background/crowd characters, distant LODs, cinematics with a fixed camera and known action, and any character whose cloth does not need to react to unpredictable gameplay. Requires a DCC cloth bake and an import path. Not applicable where cloth must react to gameplay: wind from explosions, character contact, vehicle motion, or player-driven poses.
cloth_baked_animation.limitations: Baked cloth cannot respond to anything unscripted: it will intersect the character after a teleport, a speed change, or any animation blend not covered by the bake.
