Storage: per-frame or per-animation cloth data adds to animation memory/disk. Iteration cost: every animation retake requires a re-bake. Art-side, the fallback is visible if the switch distance is inside the camera's inspection range.
cloth_baked_animation.required_data_and_tools: A DCC cloth solver for baking (or an offline simulation of the in-game solver), an import/playback path for baked cloth (animation bones or vertex cache), LOD/significance switching logic, and a review process for the switch distance.

impact.cpu: high reduction vs simulation (no solver step); baked motion rides on the existing animation evaluation
impact.gpu: low-medium reduction (no extra simulation passes); cost moves into standard skinning or a vertex-texture fetch
impact.ram: low per instance; medium in total if many baked animations are resident
impact.vram: low-medium (baked animation textures if the vertex-cache path is used)
impact.network: none

cloth_baked_animation.quality_impact: High quality for scripted content (offline solvers produce better cloth than real-time ones). Negative for unscripted interaction: cloth will not react to gameplay events and may visibly intersect geometry.
cloth_baked_animation.concept_impact: Low-medium. It makes cloth viable on characters that could not otherwise afford it, which lets art dress background crowds; but it forecloses gameplay-reactive cloth.

effort_person_days.formula: p50 = 1 (bake/import path) + 1.5 (LOD/significance switch integration) + 1 (playback validation on N animations) + 0.5 (memory/disk budget check) = 4; p80 = p50 x 2.25 = 9 (re-bakes after animation retakes and intersection fixes dominate). Excludes authoring the cloth itself.

dependencies: An animation/skinning pipeline that can carry the baked cloth (extra bones or vertex cache)
A LOD/significance metric for the switch

relations.note: Baked motion vs runtime constraint solve; most projects use both, selected by distance/importance.
Both are LOD fallbacks replacing a per-element simulation with pre-authored approximations.
Same principle - pre-authored states played back instead of runtime simulation - applied to damage rather than cloth.

cloth_baked_animation.verification: For each baked animation, run an automated intersection check: sample the character's cloth vertices against its collision capsules across the animation and count penetrating frames (target: zero beyond a small tolerance). Then run a LOD-switch review: record a camera dolly through the switch distance on 10 characters and confirm no visible motion discontinuity. Finally, compare frame time with baked vs simulated cloth on a scene with the design maximum number of cloth characters.

claims.statement: Unreal's Chaos Cloth documentation defines Max Distance as 'the maximum distance any point on the cloth can move from its animated position', with Backstop Distance and Backstop Radius further constraining movement - i.e. the authored animation is the reference that simulation is bounded against.
claims.locator: Section 'Masks' - Max Distance / Backstop Distance / Backstop Radius

claims.statement: Unreal documents Anim Drive Multiplier as driving 'springs that pull clothing towards its animated position, giving control to animators in cinematics or animation-driven scenes', and notes it can be driven at runtime and combines multiplicatively with painted values.
In Unreal's cloth painting, a paint value of 0 means the skinned vertex could not move (fully bound to animation) and 100 allows the skinned vertex to move one metre from its original position.

Epic's groom documentation lists 'Groom Caches - An overview of using imported Groom Caches with grooms', confirming the imported-cache playback pattern exists in-engine for strand data; the analogous cloth path is expert_estimate.
No published measurement of the CPU/GPU saving from baked vs simulated cloth was found in this pass; the impact bands are derived from the mechanism.

game_examples.fact: Demonstrates the underlying principle for character presentation: the Body subsystem 'owns animation state' separately from Locomotion, Vision and Intention, and climbing uses a pick from 'dozens of motion captured climb animations of various height increments' - i.e. authored/captured motion played back rather than solved at runtime.
game_examples.non_transferable: This is authored animation for locomotion, not baked cloth. It confirms the project's preference for pre-authored motion playback, not any cloth-specific technique or cost.

cloth_constraint_simulation.problem: Cloth that is skinned to the skeleton cannot respond to wind, player motion, or contact, so capes, coats, flags and drapery look rigid and intersect the body. A runtime constraint solver (mass-spring / position-based dynamics) resolves this, but it adds a per-frame solve over hundreds to thousands of particles per character and is sensitive to frame time, collisions and stretching.

implementation_variants.name: Engine particle-solver cloth with painted per-vertex influence (Unreal Chaos Cloth)
implementation_variants.description: Cloth is authored in-editor: a cloth asset is created from a Skeletal Mesh LOD section, influence is painted per vertex, and a low-level particle solver simulates it. Movement is bounded by painted masks (Max Distance, Backstop Distance/Radius) and animators can pull cloth back toward the animation with Anim Drive springs.

implementation_variants.name: Cloth driven by a physics asset for collision, iterated solver with stiffness/damping presets
implementation_variants.description: The cloth asset references the character's Physics Asset so simulated particles collide with the body; the Cloth Config exposes material presets (burlap, rubber, etc.) that map to solver stiffness/damping/iteration behaviour.

implementation_variants.name: DCC-authored cloth (PhysX DCC plugin in 3ds Max / Maya) imported as simulation data
implementation_variants.description: The pre-Unreal standard workflow: cloth is authored in a DCC tool using NVIDIA's PhysX DCC plugin and imported. Unreal's paint tool is explicitly designed to feel familiar to users of that workflow, and cloth setups can be copied between similar Skeletal Meshes rather than rebuilt.

implementation_variants.name: Constrained/reduced cloth: cap max distance, disable simulation by distance or LOD, swap to baked animation
implementation_variants.description: The budget-control variant: bound the solve with per-vertex Max Distance so it can never run away, disable simulation on distant or offscreen characters, and fall back to baked or purely skinned cloth. This pairing is why cloth_baked_animation is modelled as a sibling method rather than an alternative discipline.

cloth_constraint_simulation.applicability_conditions: Requires a skinned character or object with a garment/drape that must react to motion or wind, and a budget for a per-character solve. Needs a Physics Asset (or equivalent collision proxy) for believable self/body collision. Practical when the number of simultaneously simulated cloth instances is small (hero characters, a handful of NPCs), and when the art direction accepts bounded motion.
cloth_constraint_simulation.limitations: Cost is per simulated instance, so it does not scale to crowds without a disable policy. Cloth is a spring system: it stretches under large timestep spikes and can explode if velocities are unclamped, which is why Max Distance / backstop masks exist. Interpenetration with the body is only as good as the collision proxy. Determinism and networked replication of cloth are generally not solved by the solver, so cloth is usually cosmetic-only and client-local. Authoring cost is real: each garment is hand-painted and tuned.
cloth_constraint_simulation.required_data_and_tools: Skeletal mesh with an LOD section to derive cloth from; a Physics Asset for collision; a cloth paint tool (in-editor or DCC); solver parameter sets (stiffness, damping, iterations); a debug view for particle positions and collision; a test rig exercising fast rotation, teleport, and time-scale changes.

impact.cpu: medium-high (a solver step over N particles per simulated instance, several constraint iterations per step); grows linearly with simultaneously simulated instances unless disabled
impact.gpu: low (result is written into the skinned vertex buffer); higher if skinning is GPU-side and the cloth result must be uploaded per frame
impact.ram: low-medium (particle state + constraints per instance; roughly proportional to simulated vertex count)
impact.vram: low (cloth result is part of the skinned mesh buffers)
impact.disk: low (paint masks and config; small compared with textures)
impact.network: none if cloth is cosmetic and client-local; non-trivial if it must be authoritative or replicated

cloth_constraint_simulation.quality_impact: Directly visible: garments and drapery respond to movement, wind and contact instead of clipping through the body. Quality is bounded by authoring skill and by the collision proxy; badly tuned cloth reads worse than rigid cloth.
cloth_constraint_simulation.concept_impact: Enables art direction that depends on fabric motion (long coats, banners, capes as silhouette). It does not change core mechanics; it is presentation-layer, unless physics-driven cloth occlusion or drag is a mechanic.

effort_person_days.formula: p50 = 3 (solver integration + component wiring) + 2 (Physics Asset collision authoring for the first garment) + 3 (paint + tune the first garment to shippable quality) + 2 (per-garment reuse pipeline: copy/setup) + 2 (budget policy: disable by distance/LOD + profiling) = 12 for 1-3 garments on an existing engine solver; p80 = p50 x ~2.2 (per-garment tuning loops and collision-proxy rework dominate) = 26. Excludes writing a solver from scratch (add 20-40).

dependencies: A skinned mesh pipeline with LODs
A physics asset / collision proxy for the character
A per-frame CPU or GPU budget for simulation

relations.note: Baking trades responsiveness for near-zero runtime cost; the two are usually combined by distance/importance, not chosen once globally.
Spring-based cloth is timestep-sensitive; a stable fixed step or substepping is required to avoid stretching and explosions.
Both are per-entity soft-body solves with LOD and budget controls; skills and budget policy transfer, solvers do not.
The same disable-by-distance policy that parks rigid bodies also parks cloth instances.

cloth_constraint_simulation.verification: Measure per-instance solver time in a scene with the maximum expected number of simulated garments active, and assert it stays under the allocated per-frame budget at p99 over a 10-minute soak. Separately, run a stress rig: teleport the character, rotate at high angular velocity, and pause/resume; assert no particle exceeds its Max Distance mask and no NaNs enter the vertex buffer. Visually verify no body interpenetration at the authored contact poses.

claims.statement: Unreal Engine uses the Chaos Cloth solver, described as a low-level clothing solver responsible for the particle simulation that runs clothing, chosen so integrations are lightweight and extensible because there is direct access to the simulation data.
Cloth is authored in-editor: a cloth asset is created from a Skeletal Mesh LOD section ('Create Cloth Asset from Selection') and assigned to the render mesh, then influence is painted per vertex.
claims.locator: 'Create and Assign a Cloth Asset' steps 3-4

claims.statement: The brush Paint Value controls how much a painted area reacts like cloth: a value of 0 means the skinned vertex cannot move, and a value of 100 allows the skinned vertex to move one meter from its original position.

Cloth parameters are exposed as swappable Masks (parameter sets) with Targets: Max Distance (maximum distance any point on the cloth can move from its animated position), Backstop Distance, Backstop Radius (a sphere that prevents painted points entering a region), and Anim Drive Multiplier (springs pulling clothing towards its animated position). Only one of each target can be assigned at a time, enabling non-destructive A/B testing.

Anim Drive Multiplier can be driven at runtime from Blueprints via the interactor object on Skeletal Mesh Components; the runtime value is multiplicatively combined with the painted values to produce final spring and damper strengths.
When creating a cloth asset for a character, the documentation instructs the user to supply the character's Physics Asset to get proper collision for the cloth simulation.
claims.locator: 'Create and Assign a Cloth Asset', 'Physics Asset' bullet

claims.statement: Unreal's cloth paint controls are stated to feel familiar to users of NVIDIA's PhysX DCC Plugin for 3ds Max or Maya, indicating the in-editor workflow is a deliberate replacement for DCC-authored cloth.
No published per-instance cloth solve cost, particle count, or frame-time figure was found in the verified primary sources; the cost band above is an expert estimate, not a measurement.
claims.locator: whole page - no performance figures present

game_examples.game: Unreal Engine shipped titles using Chaos Cloth
game_examples.fact: The engine ships a documented, in-editor cloth authoring and simulation pipeline (Chaos Cloth solver, painted masks with Max Distance / Backstop / Anim Drive targets, Physics-Asset-driven collision) rather than each studio writing its own solver.
game_examples.non_transferable: This confirms the technique is productionised in a shipping engine, but it is not a specific game, and no cost, particle count or visual result transfers to another title. The engine feature existing says nothing about whether a given project can afford it.

destruction_geometry_cache.problem: Simulating destruction live costs rigid-body time for every fragment and is non-deterministic to author against; but pre-baking an entire destruction sequence costs memory and disk. A geometry cache records the per-frame transforms and events of a simulation once, then replays them, decoupling runtime cost from fragment count.

implementation_variants.name: Record-and-replay cache (Unreal Chaos Cache / Geometry Collection caching)
implementation_variants.description: The destruction system captures per-frame transforms and events and reduces the destruction data for efficient storage and replay. Cached simulations can remain interactive because parts of the simulation can become live again on interaction.

implementation_variants.name: Pre-fractured Geometry Collections with clustering
implementation_variants.description: Destruction is authored offline: geometry is fractured into a Geometry Collection and grouped into clusters that break apart progressively under damage. Runtime only has to un-cluster and then simulate, or replay, the authored result.

implementation_variants.name: Budgeted cache with published per-asset memory targets
implementation_variants.description: Rainbow Six Siege documents explicit destruction budgets per destructible: roughly 6 ms of simulation for a wall, about 25 MB of GPU memory and about 200 MB of data plus 150 MB of engine overhead in RAM, showing that cache size is a designed budget line, not an emergent property.

implementation_variants.name: Voxel-based destruction with full runtime modification
implementation_variants.description: The opposite pole: Teardown's engine is voxel-based, so destruction is a structural modification of the world rather than a cached simulation. This is cited here as a contrasting architecture, documented only from a studio year-summary blog post.

destruction_geometry_cache.applicability_conditions: Use when destruction is a scripted or repeatable set-piece, when the fragment count is too high to simulate live, when determinism or replay (for networking or killcams) matters, or when the target platform cannot afford live rigid-body simulation. Requires that the break pattern can be pre-authored, i.e. the destroyed object and the impact are known in advance or parameterisable.
destruction_geometry_cache.limitations: A cache cannot respond to arbitrary new impacts unless the design explicitly re-enters live simulation at a seam (which Chaos supports per the 'become live upon interaction' note, but each seam is extra complexity). Cache size grows with fragment count, frame count and playback rate, so long or high-fragment-count sequences become a disk and memory line item. Pre-fracturing is an art task and changes level-authoring workflow. A cached sequence looks identical every time unless variants are authored.
destruction_geometry_cache.required_data_and_tools: An offline simulation bake step (editor or build farm); a cache asset format with compression; clustering/fracture authoring tools; a streaming policy for loading caches; profiling to attribute cache size per level; a determinism check if caches are replayed in multiplayer.

impact.cpu: low at runtime (transform playback instead of simulation) versus medium-high for live simulation; the saving is exactly the simulation cost that was avoided
impact.gpu: low-medium (fragments still render; cost is driven by visible fragment count and draw/material setup, not by whether they are cached)
impact.ram: medium-high (cache data resident); Rainbow Six Siege publishes roughly 200 MB of data plus 150 MB of engine overhead as its destruction RAM budget
impact.vram: medium (fragment meshes and cache buffers); Rainbow Six Siege publishes about 25 MB of GPU memory for destruction
impact.disk: medium-high (baked caches are stored on disk and scale with number of destructibles x sequence length)
impact.network: low and beneficial: a cached, deterministic sequence is easier to replicate than a live simulation, but the cache must be present on all clients

destruction_geometry_cache.quality_impact: Allows far higher fragment counts and more spectacular authored destruction than could be simulated live, and makes the result repeatable and art-directable. The risk is visible repetition and the loss of true player-driven variability.
destruction_geometry_cache.concept_impact: Enables destruction as a designed gameplay space (breach points, sightline creation) because the outcome is predictable and authorable. It constrains emergent destruction, which matters if emergent destruction is the pitch.

effort_person_days.formula: p50 = 4 (bake pipeline: record simulation -> cache asset -> validation) + 4 (cache streaming + memory budgeting) + 4 (fracture/cluster authoring guidelines for one asset class, e.g. walls) + 3 (interactive re-entry: cache -> live seam) + 3 (tooling for artists to bake and preview) = 18; p80 = p50 x ~2.2 (per-asset-class authoring cost and cache-size blowups dominate; Rainbow Six Siege's published budgets imply a sustained budgeting effort) = 40.

dependencies: A destruction/fracture authoring pipeline
A simulation that can be run offline and recorded
A memory and disk budget allocated to caches

relations.note: Caching removes cost from the steady state; a runtime fracture budget still bounds the parts that must stay live. They solve different halves of the same problem.
Both are budget-oriented destructible policies; if you already bound live fracture tightly you may not need caching, and vice versa.
Fragments that have come to rest should be parked by the same deactivation policy as other rigid bodies; otherwise the cache saving is lost to still-simulating debris.
A cache recorded at one timestep and replayed at another will drift or pop; the bake step and runtime step must agree.

destruction_geometry_cache.verification: Compare runtime cost of the same destructible in cached vs live mode and record the delta in ms and in resident bytes. Then measure cache size per destructible against an allocated per-level budget and fail the build when exceeded. Finally, verify interactive re-entry: strike a cached destructible at a seam and confirm the affected sub-part goes live while the rest continues playing back, with no visible duplication or pop.

claims.statement: Unreal's destruction cache system captures per-frame transforms and events and reduces the destruction data for efficient storage and replay capabilities.
Cached destruction simulations are documented as still being interactive, because certain parts of the simulation can become live upon interaction.
Rainbow Six Siege budgets roughly 6 ms of simulation time for a destructible wall.
claims.locator: GDC 2016 slide deck, destruction budget slide ('roughly 6ms for a wall')

claims.statement: Rainbow Six Siege allocated about 25 MB of GPU memory to destruction.
claims.locator: GDC 2016 slide deck, destruction budget slide ('GPU memory: 25 MB')

claims.statement: Rainbow Six Siege allocated about 200 MB of data plus 150 MB of engine overhead in RAM to destruction.
claims.locator: GDC 2016 slide deck, destruction budget slide ('RAM: 200 MB data + 150 MB engine')

claims.statement: The Rainbow Six Siege figures are that game's published budgets for its own destructible scope and console targets; they are not a target another project should copy, because fragment counts, art density and platform differ.

Unreal's documented destruction workflow is authored around Geometry Collections (authoring, fracture, clustering, selection tools) with a dedicated Fracture Mode and Dataflow graph option, i.e. destruction is an offline authoring discipline first and a runtime system second.
claims.locator: 'Key Concepts' link list (Geometry Collections User Guide, Fracturing Geometry Collections, Cluster Geometry Collections, Dataflow for Destruction Quickstart)

game_examples.fact: The team published hard destruction budgets - roughly 6 ms of simulation for a wall, about 25 MB GPU memory, about 200 MB of data plus 150 MB engine overhead in RAM - and treat destruction as a designed, budgeted system with asynchronous event listeners.
game_examples.locator: GDC 2016 slide deck, destruction budget slide
game_examples.non_transferable: These are Siege's own budgets for its destructible scope (mostly walls/hatches) on its target consoles. They do not transfer as targets: a game with whole-building destruction, a different fragmentation density, or a different platform has a completely different budget. The transferable lesson is that the budget exists and is published per asset class.

game_examples.fact: The studio's engine is voxel-based, so destruction is structural modification of the world rather than a pre-fractured, cached simulation - the contrasting architecture to a geometry cache.
game_examples.non_transferable: This is the opposite approach, not an instance of geometry caching. A voxel world has different memory and authoring characteristics entirely; nothing about Teardown's performance or visual result transfers to a mesh-fracture pipeline. Also note this was verified only from a studio year-summary blog post, not a technical paper.

runtime_fracture_budget.problem: Procedural runtime fracture produces an unbounded number of rigid bodies exactly when the frame is already stressed (explosions, collisions). Without an explicit budget - maximum fragments, maximum live simulation time, damage thresholds and cluster depth - a single event can spawn thousands of bodies and stall the frame.

implementation_variants.name: Cluster/damage-threshold fracture with progressive un-clustering
implementation_variants.description: Geometry is pre-clustered; damage propagates and breaks clusters apart progressively rather than exploding straight to leaf fragments. Physics Fields can break Geometry Collection clusters or anchor/disable fractured bodies, which is the engine-side mechanism for keeping fragment counts bounded.

implementation_variants.name: Hard caps: max live fragments, max live simulation time, oldest-fragment recycling
implementation_variants.description: A global budget on simultaneously simulated fragments, with the oldest or least visible fragments removed, merged or frozen when the cap is hit. The R6 Siege 'roughly 6ms for a wall' figure is an example of this kind of budget being made explicit and enforced per asset class.

implementation_variants.name: Event-driven fracture driven by physics fields, with Niagara reacting to break events
implementation_variants.description: Fracture is triggered and shaped by physics fields (force, break, anchor, disable) rather than by spawning bodies directly; rendering reacts via break and collision events so the number of visible effects is decoupled from the number of simulated bodies.

implementation_variants.name: Toolkit-level fracture authoring with a damage model (NVIDIA Blast)
implementation_variants.description: Use an open SDK (NVIDIA Blast) that provides the fracture authoring and runtime damage model rather than building it. Cited here as the build-vs-buy option; only the repository's existence and scope were verified, not any performance figure.

runtime_fracture_budget.applicability_conditions: Any title where destruction happens during gameplay rather than in a cut-scene, and where the fragment count cannot be fully predicted at authoring time. Necessary when the destruction is player-triggered and therefore can be spammed. Less necessary when every destruction event is authored and can be cached instead.
runtime_fracture_budget.limitations: Budgets are content-dependent: a fragment count that is safe for a small prop is not safe for a building. Caps create visible artefacts (fragments disappearing, freezing, or popping) that must be hidden by effects. Damage-threshold tuning is iterative and per material. Runtime fracture is harder to make deterministic than cached fracture, which complicates networking and replay.
runtime_fracture_budget.required_data_and_tools: A fracture/authoring toolkit (Geometry Collections, NVIDIA Blast, or in-house); an instrumented counter for live fragment count and per-frame destruction simulation time; a stress scene that triggers maximum simultaneous destruction; a policy for recycling/deactivating fragments integrated with the physics LOD system.

impact.cpu: medium-high without a budget; the point of the method is to convert an unbounded cost into a bounded one. The R6 Siege figure of roughly 6 ms for a wall is a published example of the bounded value.
impact.gpu: medium (fragment draw count and shadow/visibility cost scale with live fragments)
impact.ram: medium (per-fragment body state); bounded by the cap
impact.vram: low-medium (fragment meshes; usually instanced from a small set)
impact.disk: low (fracture data is authored once; runtime fracture generates state, not assets)
impact.network: medium risk: runtime fracture is hard to make deterministic, so it must either be server-authoritative with result replication or accepted as cosmetic and divergent

runtime_fracture_budget.quality_impact: With a well-tuned budget, destruction looks rich while staying smooth. With a badly tuned one, players see fragments vanish or freeze - a directly readable failure. The budget is therefore a quality parameter, not just a performance one.
runtime_fracture_budget.concept_impact: Determines whether destruction can be a core, repeatable mechanic (breaching, cover denial) or must be a spectacle. An unbounded-fracture design cannot be shipped on a fixed frame budget.

effort_person_days.formula: p50 = 4 (fragment/live-body counters and per-frame instrumentation) + 3 (global cap + recycling policy) + 3 (damage threshold and cluster-depth tuning for one material class) + 3 (integration with physics deactivation/LOD) + 2 (stress scene + automated budget regression) = 15; p80 = p50 x ~2.1 (tuning per material class and hiding the artefacts of recycling dominate) = 32. Assumes an existing fracture system; excludes building one.

dependencies: A destruction/fracture system that can be instrumented
A physics LOD / deactivation policy for fragments
A per-frame CPU budget allocated to destruction

relations.note: Caching bounds the authored cases; a runtime budget bounds the emergent ones. A shipped destruction system normally needs both.
Fragments at rest must actually stop costing; without deactivation the fragment cap only delays the stall.
A few thousand small fragments is precisely the workload a good broadphase exists to absorb; a bad one makes the budget unachievable.
Fragment and debris pools share the same allocation-avoidance discipline as particle pools.

runtime_fracture_budget.verification: Build a stress scene that triggers the maximum simultaneous destruction the design allows (worst case: several destructibles in one frame). Record peak live fragment count and peak destruction simulation ms; assert both stay under cap and that the game never exceeds its frame budget at p99. Then run a 10-minute soak in which destruction is triggered repeatedly and assert live fragment count returns to baseline (no leak) and that recycled fragments are covered by an effect or are offscreen.

claims.statement: Unreal's Physics Fields can affect simulation in ways that bound fracture: exerting force on rigid bodies, breaking Geometry Collection clusters, and anchoring or disabling fractured rigid bodies.

Niagara can read Chaos Destruction Break Events and Collision Events to spawn particles or modify an existing particle system at runtime, which decouples visual effect count from simulated body count.

Rainbow Six Siege enforces a per-asset-class destruction budget of roughly 6 ms of simulation for a wall, demonstrating that runtime fracture cost is treated as an explicit, authored budget rather than an emergent cost.

Rainbow Six Siege's destruction documentation explicitly warns that some care is needed to have asynchronous listeners for destruction events, i.e. gameplay/AI reactions to destruction must not be synchronous with the fracture.
claims.locator: GDC 2016 deck, 'Hint: some care needed to have asynchronous listeners'

claims.statement: No published figure for maximum live fragment count, cluster depth, or fracture ms on a specified hardware target was found in the verified sources beyond the single R6 Siege wall budget; fragment caps must be derived by measurement on the target project.
claims.locator: Chaos Destruction index page - no numeric budgets published

game_examples.fact: Destruction is budgeted per asset class (roughly 6 ms for a wall) and destruction listeners are asynchronous; AI visibility through partially broken walls is a documented consequence of the system.
game_examples.locator: GDC 2016 deck, budget slide and AI-visibility slide
game_examples.non_transferable: The 6 ms figure is Siege's own budget for its own destructible scope on its own hardware. It is not a target for another game. What transfers is the practice: publish and enforce a per-asset-class budget, and make destruction event handling asynchronous.

hair_cards_lod.problem: Strand-level hair is expensive and, on some platforms, unsupported. Card-based hair (textured quads carrying hair clusters) is the traditional real-time approximation, but it must be generated, LOD'd, and swapped against strands, otherwise it either looks like a flat texture or costs as much as strands.

implementation_variants.name: Cards/meshes assigned to LOD levels, strands reserved for the closest LOD
implementation_variants.description: Unreal's groom system explicitly supports both representations - 'Traditionally, hair created for use in real-time projects has been created using card-based techniques, or other similar approximations. The groom system in Unreal Engine manages and utilizes these methods, as well.' - with dedicated pages for setting up LOD groups and for setting up cards and meshes per LOD.

implementation_variants.name: Engine-side LOD system in the hair SDK itself
implementation_variants.description: TressFX 4.1 introduced a 'New Level of Detail (LOD) system' as a headline feature, i.e. LOD is handled inside the hair technology rather than being bolted on by the game.

implementation_variants.name: Scalability-driven degradation (disable strands, reduce MSAA/PPLL samples)
implementation_variants.description: Rather than swapping geometry, degrade the strand pipeline per platform: Unreal's groom scalability documentation warns strands require an allocated performance budget and are not supported on all platforms, and exposes MSAA sample counts (default 4, up to 8) and PPLL sample counts (up to 32, very expensive) as quality knobs.

implementation_variants.name: Generated card textures from the groom (follicle/strand textures)
implementation_variants.description: Cards are made convincing by baking the groom into textures: Unreal documents generation of follicle and strand textures for groom assets and a hair card generator workflow.

hair_cards_lod.applicability_conditions: Any project with human (or furred) characters that must hold up at medium and long camera distances, or that targets platforms where strand rendering is not viable. Mandatory when the character count on screen is high. Cards are the default when the target hardware has no strand budget at all.
hair_cards_lod.limitations: Cards read as flat at close range and on silhouettes; they alias and shimmer without careful mip/alpha handling. Swapping strands to cards produces a visible pop unless the transition is masked by distance, camera framing or an effect. Card authoring is art work per groom. Strand-to-card parity is never exact, so a character can subtly change identity across the swap.
hair_cards_lod.required_data_and_tools: A groom authoring pipeline (XGen/Maya or equivalent, exported as Alembic); a card generator or hand-authored cards; LOD group setup per groom; generated follicle/strand textures; a platform capability matrix stating which platforms get strands; a test scene with a controlled camera dolly to inspect the swap distance.

impact.cpu: low (card hair is geometry; the saving versus strands is mostly GPU, plus less simulation if strands were simulated)
impact.gpu: low-medium for cards versus high for strands; cards are cheap alpha-tested geometry while strands pay a strand rasterisation and, with MSAA/PPLL, a resolve cost
impact.ram: low (a card mesh and its textures per groom)
impact.vram: low-medium (card textures; much smaller than the per-strand buffers and PPLL lists)
impact.disk: low-medium (card meshes + baked textures per groom)
impact.network: none

hair_cards_lod.quality_impact: High leverage: with good cards and a well-placed swap, distant and crowd characters look correct at a fraction of strand cost. With a badly placed swap, the character visibly simplifies in view, which is worse than never using strands.
hair_cards_lod.concept_impact: Determines whether a game can feature many groomed characters at all. Card LOD is usually what makes a crowd of groomed humans affordable.

effort_person_days.formula: p50 = 3 (LOD group setup per groom + platform capability matrix) + 4 (card generation/bake pipeline and texture generation for the first groom) + 3 (per-groom card authoring/cleanup for 2-3 grooms) + 2 (swap-distance tuning + pop mitigation) + 2 (scalability settings per platform) = 14; p80 = p50 x ~2.1 (per-groom art cleanup and platform matrix expansion dominate) = 30. Excludes building a card generator.

dependencies: A groom asset pipeline (strand source data)
An LOD system that can swap groom representations
A platform capability matrix

relations.note: Cards are the LOD fallback for strands; a complete hair solution is strands-near + cards-far, not one or the other.
On platforms without a strand budget, cards are the only option - a hard platform constraint, not a stylistic preference.
Both are 'replace expensive geometry with a cheap textured proxy at distance' and share the pop-mitigation problem.
Both are bake-away-the-simulation strategies selected by distance/importance.

hair_cards_lod.verification: Dolly a camera from close-up to the maximum crowd viewing distance on the lowest target platform and record: the distance at which the strand-to-card swap happens, whether the swap is perceptible in a side-by-side frame capture, and the GPU ms saved by running cards at that distance. Assert that on any platform in the no-strand list, cards (not strands) are selected automatically.

claims.statement: Epic states that hair for real-time projects has traditionally been created using card-based techniques or other similar approximations, and that Unreal's groom system manages and utilizes these methods as well as strand-based workflows.

The Unreal groom documentation ships dedicated pages for setting up level of detail groups for grooms and for setting up cards and meshes for grooms, i.e. cards and meshes are assigned to LOD levels of the same groom asset.
claims.locator: 'Additional Topics' links: 'Setting Up Level of Detail for Grooms' and 'Setting Up Cards and Meshes for Grooms'

claims.statement: Unreal documents generation of follicle and strand textures for groom assets and provides a hair card generator topic, i.e. card appearance is baked from the groom rather than hand-painted from scratch.
TressFX 4.1 lists a 'New Level of Detail (LOD) system' among its headline new features, alongside optimized physics simulation shaders.
Unreal's groom scalability documentation states that strand rendering requires an allocated performance budget and is not supported on all platforms, which forces card fallback on some targets.
claims.locator: 'Groom Scalability and Performance' - strand budget/platform support statements

claims.statement: Unreal's groom scalability exposes MSAA with a default of 4 samples and up to 8, and PPLL with up to 32 samples described as very expensive - quality knobs that interact with whether strands are affordable at all.
claims.locator: 'Groom Scalability and Performance' - MSAA/PPLL sample settings

claims.statement: No published measurement of the GPU cost difference between card hair and strand hair on a specified platform was found in the verified sources; the cost bands above are expert estimates.

game_examples.fact: Unreal's own groom documentation illustrates a MetaHuman character with grooms rendered as strands (left) and as cards (right), i.e. Epic's reference character pipeline ships both representations of the same groom.
game_examples.locator: 'Hair Rendering and Simulation' figure caption: 'MetaHuman character example with grooms showing their strands (left) and cards (right).'
game_examples.non_transferable: This confirms the dual-representation workflow is shipped by Epic, but it is an engine demo asset, not a game shipping on a specific platform. No cost, hair count, or swap distance transfers.

hair_strand_simulation.problem: Card hair cannot deliver per-strand motion or silhouette detail. Strand-based hair renders and simulates individual curves, which is the current fidelity ceiling, but it is costly, platform-gated, and needs both a render budget and a simulation budget.

implementation_variants.name: Strand-based groom with per-strand physics (Unreal groom system)
implementation_variants.description: Unreal's groom system uses a strand-based workflow to render each individual strand with physically accurate motion, targeting hundreds of thousands or more strands in real time, with a dedicated page for enabling and configuring physics on grooms and for groom interpolation (how curves move with respect to skinned meshes and physics simulation).

implementation_variants.name: GPU compute strand physics with constraint solving (TressFX)
implementation_variants.description: TressFX is AMD's hair/fur rendering and simulation technology designed to use the GPU to simulate and render high-quality hair; 4.1 advertises optimized physics simulation shaders allowing more hair to be simulated in real time, via faster Velocity Shock Propagation, simplified Local Shape Constraints, and a reorganization of dispatches.

implementation_variants.name: Guide-hair simulation with interpolation of the rest of the groom
implementation_variants.description: Simulate a small subset of guide strands and interpolate the remainder. Unreal documents groom interpolation as the mechanism defining how a groom's curves move with respect to skinned meshes and physics simulation, which is the standard shape of this approach; the specific guide ratio is a project parameter and is expert_estimate here.

implementation_variants.name: Groom caches (baked simulation replay)
implementation_variants.description: Unreal documents imported Groom Caches as an alternative to live simulation - the same record-and-replay trade as cloth baking and destruction caching.

hair_strand_simulation.applicability_conditions: Use for hero characters viewed at close range where hair motion is part of the performance (cut-scenes, dialogue, character creators). Requires a strand-capable platform and an explicit performance budget. Not applicable to crowds unless combined with card LOD or a very small strand budget.
hair_strand_simulation.limitations: Epic states strands require an allocated performance budget and are not supported on all platforms. Anti-aliasing is a first-class cost: MSAA defaults to 4 samples (up to 8) and PPLL goes to 32 samples and is described as very expensive. Simulation is timestep-sensitive and can jitter. Authoring requires a groom pipeline (Alembic, XGen guidelines). Strand hair also interacts with transparency/AA and post-process in ways that are hard to debug late.
hair_strand_simulation.required_data_and_tools: A groom authoring and export pipeline (Alembic for Grooms specification, XGen guidelines); a strand-capable renderer with MSAA/PPLL configuration; a physics configuration for grooms; binding to the skeletal mesh; a budgeting pass measuring GPU ms per groom at the worst camera distance; a platform capability matrix.

impact.cpu: low-medium (binding, interpolation, and any CPU-side simulation; GPU-based solvers push this down)
impact.gpu: high (strand rasterisation plus AA resolve; PPLL up to 32 samples is documented as very expensive)
impact.ram: low-medium (groom asset data; interpolation data)
impact.vram: medium-high (strand buffers and, if used, per-pixel linked-list memory)
impact.network: none; hair is cosmetic and client-local

hair_strand_simulation.quality_impact: Highest-fidelity hair available in real time; per-strand motion is legible in close-ups and in silhouette. Wrongly configured, it produces shimmer, aliasing and a visible performance cliff.
hair_strand_simulation.concept_impact: Enables character-driven games that sell on facial and hair fidelity (narrative titles, character creators). It does not change mechanics.

effort_person_days.formula: p50 = 3 (enable strands + import/bind first groom) + 3 (physics configuration and interpolation setup) + 4 (AA/scalability tuning: MSAA/PPLL across platforms) + 3 (per-groom budget pass and shader/overdraw triage) + 3 (card LOD pairing so strands are only used near) = 16; p80 = p50 x ~2.1 (AA/aliasing iteration and platform-specific degradation dominate) = 34. Excludes writing a strand renderer.

dependencies: A groom asset pipeline with Alembic export
A strand-capable platform and an allocated GPU budget
Card/mesh LOD fallback for platforms or distances without a strand budget

relations.note: Strands are only viable if a cheaper representation exists for distance and for unsupported platforms.
Both are per-entity soft-body solves with LOD and budget controls; the discipline transfers, the solvers do not.
Strand physics is a spring system; variable timesteps produce jitter and stretching.
For distant characters, an impostor/card proxy is a cheaper answer than a strand budget that scales with character count.

hair_strand_simulation.verification: Measure GPU ms attributable to hair by toggling strand rendering on/off at the worst-case camera distance and character count, on the lowest target platform. Assert the delta fits the allocated budget with the chosen MSAA/PPLL settings. Then run a motion test (fast head turns, jumps) and assert no strand jitter, no popping at the strand-to-card swap distance, and no NaN/exploding strands after a pause/resume or timescale change.

claims.statement: Unreal's groom rendering and simulation system uses a strand-based workflow to render each individual strand of hair with physically accurate motion, enabling artists to simulate and render hundreds of thousands (or more) photo-real hairs in real-time.
Unreal's groom scalability documentation states that strands require an allocated performance budget and are not supported on all platforms.

claims.statement: In Unreal's groom scalability settings, MSAA defaults to 4 samples and can be raised up to 8.

TressFX is AMD's hair/fur rendering and simulation technology designed to use the GPU to simulate and render high-quality, realistic hair and fur; version 4.1 advertises optimized physics simulation shaders 'allowing more hair to be simulated in real-time'.
