flipbook_particles.problem: A volumetric or fluid effect that looks right may be unaffordable at runtime on the target device. Baking the simulation into a tiled flipbook texture and replaying it on a cheap sprite emitter replaces a simulation with a texture lookup, at the cost of losing interactivity and adding texture memory.

implementation_variants.name: Bake a Niagara simulation to a tiled flipbook and replay it on a 2D sprite emitter
implementation_variants.description: Epic's documented workflow: when an effect 'takes up too much memory' or cannot run in real time on the target platform, bake it with the Niagara Baker into a tiled image and apply it to a 2D sprite emitter, giving 'very efficient performance for games or for non-hero effects that may be farther in the background'.

implementation_variants.name: Sub UV animation module driving frame selection on a sprite renderer
implementation_variants.description: At runtime the flipbook is played by a Sub UVAnimation module in Particle Update (start/end frame) plus Sub Image Size on the Sprite Renderer, i.e. frame index arithmetic rather than simulation.

implementation_variants.name: Power-of-two atlas sizing to avoid sub-UV drift
implementation_variants.description: The documented failure mode: tile count must divide evenly into the texture size, otherwise tiles round down and leave padding, which makes the sub-UV mapping slightly off and causes the atlas to jitter as it plays. The documented fix is a power-of-two texture size with a frame-per-dimension count that divides it evenly.

implementation_variants.name: Fixed-FPS sampling with interpolation to hide low frame rates
implementation_variants.description: Godot documents the general principle for GPU particles: fixed_fps (default 30) fixes the update rate and interpolate smooths motion below the screen refresh rate - the same tactic applies when playing back a low-frame-rate flipbook.

flipbook_particles.applicability_conditions: Background, ambient, distant or non-hero effects where the viewer cannot inspect the simulation and where the effect does not need to react to the world. Especially valuable on low-end platforms and for effects that would otherwise require a fluid/grid simulation. Not applicable to hero, gameplay-critical, or highly interactive effects.
flipbook_particles.limitations: The effect is no longer simulated: it cannot react to wind, collisions, or the player, and every instance looks the same unless variants are baked. Texture memory scales with frame count times tile resolution, so long or high-resolution loops are expensive. Non-dividing tile counts cause visible jitter (documented). Baking is a build/editor step that must be re-run when the source effect changes.
flipbook_particles.required_data_and_tools: A simulation to bake (e.g. a Niagara system, optionally a Niagara Fluids grid simulation); a baker tool with camera framing, timing and texture-size controls; an atlas/sprite material with Sub UV support; a memory budget for atlases; a validation step asserting tile size divides texture size.

impact.cpu: low (frame-index arithmetic instead of simulation); the saving is the avoided simulation
impact.gpu: low (a textured sprite; cost is fill/overdraw, which still applies and can dominate for large, dense, additive sprites)
impact.ram: low (atlas residency, usually mirrored in VRAM)
impact.vram: medium (the atlas is the cost; default example is a 1024x1024 tiled texture, which scales with frames and per-tile resolution)
impact.disk: medium (baked atlas textures ship with the build)
impact.network: none

flipbook_particles.quality_impact: Looks nearly identical to the simulated original at distance and in the background; degrades on close inspection (frame stepping, lack of parallax, no interaction). Quality is a function of baked frame rate and tile resolution, both of which cost memory.
flipbook_particles.concept_impact: Lets a project keep expensive-looking ambient VFX on low-end platforms, which can preserve an art direction that would otherwise have to be cut. It cannot support VFX-as-gameplay-read (e.g. a fire that spreads).

effort_person_days.formula: p50 = 2 (baker setup: framing, timing, texture size for one effect) + 2 (Sub UV material + sprite renderer wiring) + 2 (atlas memory budget + power-of-two validation) + 2 (variant/loop-seam cleanup across 3-5 effects) = 8; p80 = p50 x ~2.25 (per-effect baking iterations and memory pressure rework dominate) = 18. Assumes an existing baker tool; excludes building one.

dependencies: A source simulation worth baking
A baker tool and an atlas material with Sub UV support
A VRAM budget allocated to effect atlases

relations.note: The bake is the fallback when GPU simulation is unaffordable on the target device; Epic frames it exactly this way.
Flipbooks are the animated case of the sprite atlas; the same power-of-two and packing discipline applies.
Flipbook emitters are usually the cheap, numerous ones, so they benefit most from pooling and instance caps.
Both replace a real simulation with a cheaper approximation that holds up only under constrained viewing conditions.

flipbook_particles.verification: Measure GPU ms and VRAM for the baked version versus the live simulation of the same effect on the lowest target platform, and record the delta. Then inspect the playing atlas at close range and assert no jitter (which indicates the tile size does not divide the texture size) and no visible loop seam. Finally, assert atlas memory across all baked effects fits the allocated VFX texture budget.

claims.statement: Epic's documented motivation for baking to a flipbook is that a Niagara effect may take up too much memory to use on a target device, and that the baked result gives very efficient performance for games or for non-hero effects that may be farther in the background.
claims.locator: intro paragraphs of 'Niagara Flipbook Baker Quick Start Guide'

claims.statement: The Niagara Baker defaults to 8 tiles along X, 8 tiles along Y, and a total texture size of 1024x1024 pixels, giving a per-tile size of 128x128 pixels.

If the number of tiles does not divide evenly into the texture size (example given: 10x10 tiles in a 1024x1024 texture), tiles are mapped at 102 px, leaving 4 extra pixels of padding at the right and bottom, which can make the sub UV mapping slightly off and cause the atlas to jitter as it plays.
claims.locator: 'Adjust the Texture Size' section, worked example

claims.statement: Epic's stated guidance for ideal behaviour is to set the texture size to a power of 2 and the frames per dimension to a number that divides evenly into that texture size.
claims.locator: 'Adjust the Texture Size' section, closing guidance

claims.statement: The Niagara System Editor defaults to 30 fps, and setting frames-per-second too low can cause the same flipbook frame to be rendered multiple times (worked example: 1 second, 30 frames captured, fps set to 20 records only 20 unique frames).

Using a baked flipbook at runtime requires a Sprite Renderer plus a Sub UVAnimation module in the Particle Update group (start/end frame) and the Sub Image Size on the sprite renderer; the example given is 8x8 = 64 frames, indexed 0 to 63.
claims.locator: 'Add the Sub UV Animation Module' and 'Adjust the Settings on the Sprite Renderer'

claims.statement: Godot documents the general mitigation for low fixed particle frame rates: fixed_fps (default 30) fixes the update rate and interpolate makes movement smoother when the fixed rate is below the screen refresh rate.
Epic states the baked approach is very efficient but publishes no measured millisecond saving or memory number for it; the saving must be measured per effect on the target device.

game_examples.game: Unreal Engine 5 projects using Niagara Fluids baked to flipbooks
game_examples.fact: Epic's own worked example bakes the Grid 3D Gas Colored Smoke Niagara Fluids template - a 3D fluid effect - to a flipbook and re-applies it to a 2D sprite emitter, explicitly because the 3D effect cannot be run in real time on the target platform.
game_examples.locator: 'Set Up the Capture' steps 1-2, and intro example paragraph
game_examples.non_transferable: This is a documented engine workflow demonstrated on a template effect, not a shipped game. The 8x8/1024 defaults and the 30 fps default are starting points, not tuned values; the actual memory and performance result for another effect or platform must be measured and does not transfer.

gpu_particle_simulation.problem: CPU particle simulation costs main-thread time per particle and becomes a bottleneck at high counts or when collision/attraction is required. Moving integration to the GPU raises the ceiling dramatically but removes CPU readback and changes the cost model from per-live-particle to per-allocated-particle.

implementation_variants.name: GPU-computed emitter with fixed allocation (Godot GPUParticles3D)
implementation_variants.description: Particles are computed on the GPU. Crucially, cost is driven by the declared amount, not the live count: 'Higher values will increase GPU requirements, even if not all particles are visible at a given time or if amount_ratio is decreased', and 'Reducing the amount_ratio has no performance benefit, since resources need to be allocated and processed for the total amount of particles regardless of the amount_ratio.'

implementation_variants.name: Reduced update rate with interpolation
implementation_variants.description: fixed_fps (default 30) fixes the particle system's update rate and interpolate smooths the result; this is the documented lever for cutting simulation cost without changing appearance much.

implementation_variants.name: Unreal Niagara GPU simulation with explicit scalability guidance
implementation_variants.description: Unreal publishes a dedicated scalability and best-practices page for Niagara, and notes that GPU simulation is not free per particle: 'a simulation of 1 particle can potentially take up the same resources as one with 64 particles', because work is dispatched in waves.

implementation_variants.name: CPU fallback for gameplay-relevant particles
implementation_variants.description: When gameplay must read or drive particles (collision callbacks against gameplay volumes, scripted single-particle emission), a CPU emitter is required; Godot documents that GPU particles offer no per-particle readback (only an aggregate AABB via capture_aabb) and that scripted emit_particle is not supported on the Compatibility renderer.

gpu_particle_simulation.applicability_conditions: High particle counts, especially with collision, attraction, or grid/fluid behaviour that is too expensive on the CPU. Requires a GPU with the needed capability (compute or transform-feedback path) and a renderer that supports it. Not applicable when gameplay logic must read individual particle state, or on renderers where the feature is unsupported.
gpu_particle_simulation.limitations: No per-particle CPU readback: Godot exposes only an aggregate AABB. GPU state is asynchronous, so restart semantics differ (the docs recommend restart() rather than toggling emitting). Allocation is per declared amount, so over-declaring wastes resources even when few particles are alive. Preprocess is a documented hazard - 'In extreme cases it can even lead to a GPU crash due to the volume of work done in a single frame'. Fill/overdraw still dominates for large translucent sprites regardless of where simulation runs.
gpu_particle_simulation.required_data_and_tools: A GPU particle path supported by the renderer; a particle-count budget and an overdraw/fill measurement (quad overdraw visualisation or GPU ms delta); a profiler that separates simulation from render cost; a fallback CPU path for gameplay-critical particles.

impact.cpu: low (CPU mostly issues dispatches and updates a few uniforms; per-particle integration moves to GPU)
impact.gpu: medium-high and driven by declared allocation and by fill/overdraw, not by live count; Unreal warns a 1-particle simulation can cost the same as a 64-particle one because of wave granularity
impact.ram: low (CPU-side parameter state only)
impact.vram: medium (particle buffers sized by declared amount)
impact.network: none; GPU particles are visual-only and client-local

gpu_particle_simulation.quality_impact: Enables an order-of-magnitude more particles and effects (collision, attraction, fluids) that are impractical on the CPU. Quality risk is fill-rate: a cheaper simulation that produces more overdraw can be slower overall.
gpu_particle_simulation.concept_impact: Enables VFX-driven readability at a scale that changes what an encounter can look like (large-scale smoke, weather, magic). If the design needs particles to be gameplay-authoritative, GPU simulation is the wrong tool.

effort_person_days.formula: p50 = 3 (enable GPU path + convert first systems) + 2 (allocation policy: declare real amounts, stop using ratio as a perf lever) + 2 (fixed_fps/interpolate tuning) + 2 (fill-rate triage on the worst view) + 1 (CPU fallback path for gameplay-driven particles) = 10; p80 = p50 x ~2.2 (per-system conversion and overdraw rework dominate) = 22. Assumes an engine that already has a GPU particle path.

dependencies: A renderer path that supports GPU particle simulation on all target platforms
A GPU budget and a fill-rate measurement method
A CPU particle path for gameplay-relevant effects

relations.note: Pooling is the CPU-side analogue of fixed GPU allocation: both exist to avoid per-frame allocation. They do not substitute for each other.
When even GPU simulation is unaffordable, bake to a flipbook - Epic's stated escalation path.
GPU simulation raises particle counts, which makes per-particle texture binding a real cost; atlases remove it.
Both are GPU-side approximations that trade physical accuracy for fill-rate-bounded cost.

gpu_particle_simulation.verification: Toggle the GPU simulation path on and off for the heaviest effect and record the GPU ms delta and the CPU ms delta separately, to confirm the cost actually moved rather than just shifted. Then sweep the declared amount and confirm cost tracks allocation, not live count (per the documented semantics). Finally, measure overdraw in the worst camera view and assert the effect is fill-bound within budget; if it is, reduce size/count rather than simulation rate.

claims.statement: Godot documents that higher 'amount' values increase GPU requirements even if not all particles are visible, and that reducing amount_ratio has no performance benefit because resources are allocated and processed for the total amount regardless.

Godot's GPU particles have fixed_fps defaulting to 30 and an interpolate flag that makes movement smoother when the fixed rate is lower than the screen refresh rate; fixed_fps does not slow the simulation itself.
For GPU particles, the only live-particle query available to the CPU is capture_aabb(), which returns the axis-aligned bounding box containing all active particles; there is no per-particle readback.

Because particles are computed on the GPU, a one-shot emitter may not restart immediately when 'emitting' is set back to true after the finished signal; the documentation recommends calling restart() instead.
claims.locator: property 'emitting' note and 'finished' signal note; method 'restart'

claims.statement: Godot warns that a high 'preprocess' value can be very expensive because it runs the particle shader once per fixed_fps step (or 30, if fixed_fps is 0) for every second preprocessed, and that in extreme cases it can lead to a GPU crash due to the volume of work done in a single frame.

Unreal's Niagara scalability documentation notes that a simulation of 1 particle can potentially take up the same resources as one with 64 particles, i.e. GPU particle cost is quantised by dispatch/wave granularity rather than strictly proportional to particle count.
claims.locator: 'Scalability and Best Practices for Niagara' - GPU simulation granularity note

claims.statement: In Godot, scripted single-particle emission via emit_particle() is only supported on the Forward+ and Mobile rendering methods, not the Compatibility renderer.

game_examples.fact: Epic publishes a dedicated Niagara scalability and best-practices page that treats GPU simulation as a scalability decision and warns that GPU particle cost is quantised (1 particle can cost the same as 64), i.e. GPU simulation is not a free win at low counts.
game_examples.non_transferable: Engine guidance, not a shipped-game measurement. The 64-particle granularity figure is specific to a GPU dispatch model and is not a portable constant; it does not transfer as a budget to another engine or hardware generation.

particle_pooling.problem: Spawning and destroying particle systems (and their emitters, buffers and components) at runtime causes allocation, garbage-collection pressure and fragmentation, producing frame spikes exactly when effects are busiest. Pooling pre-allocates a fixed set of instances and recycles them.

implementation_variants.name: Classic object pool of particle-system instances with free list
implementation_variants.description: Game Programming Patterns documents the Object Pool pattern: acquire a pre-allocated object from a pool instead of allocating, and return it instead of freeing. The pattern's own caveat is that a fixed-size pool must define behaviour when exhausted (fail, grow, or reuse the oldest).

implementation_variants.name: Fixed allocation semantics in the particle system itself
implementation_variants.description: Modern engines avoid the problem structurally by allocating the maximum particle count up front (see the GPU-particle allocation semantics) so no per-spawn allocation occurs at all - a fixed pool is effectively built into the emitter.

implementation_variants.name: Pool with capped concurrency and oldest-instance recycling
implementation_variants.description: Cap the number of concurrent instances of each effect and recycle the oldest when the cap is hit; this is the standard shipped-game shape and pairs with a significance/priority system deciding who gets the last instance. The specific cap values are project parameters and are expert_estimate here.

implementation_variants.name: Effect-level LOD: disable emitters on insignificant instances
implementation_variants.description: Unreal's Significance Manager is documented as a framework for evaluating object significance so objects can modify behaviour 'by doing things like shutting off Components like Particle Emitters, or by running complex AI code less frequently' - i.e. pooling plus significance, not pooling alone.

particle_pooling.applicability_conditions: Any game with frequent, short-lived effect spawning (shooters, action games, ability-based combat). Most valuable where the spawn rate is bursty and the frame budget is tight. Less important when effects are few, long-lived, or already backed by a fixed-allocation emitter.
particle_pooling.limitations: A pool fixes the peak, so exhaustion must be handled deliberately (drop, grow, or steal). Pooled objects must be fully reset on reuse or state leaks between uses - a classic source of 'effect plays with the wrong colour' bugs. Pooling trades steady-state memory for spike avoidance. It does not reduce fill rate or simulation cost, only allocation cost.
particle_pooling.required_data_and_tools: A pool implementation with a free list and reset-on-acquire; instrumentation for allocation counts and GC/frame spikes; a soak scene with burst spawning; a concurrency cap per effect; a debug view of pool occupancy (in use / free / peak).

impact.cpu: low-medium reduction in allocator and GC pressure; the measurable effect is fewer frame spikes, not a lower average frame time
impact.gpu: none directly (the same particles still render); indirect benefit if pooled instances let you enforce a concurrency cap
impact.ram: small increase (the pool is resident even when idle) - a deliberate trade of memory for determinism
impact.vram: small increase if pooled effects reserve GPU buffers while idle
impact.network: none

particle_pooling.quality_impact: Not visible directly; it protects the feel of the game by removing hitches during combat. Its absence is what players notice.
particle_pooling.concept_impact: None directly, but it is what allows a design with high effect density to actually ship without stutter.

effort_person_days.formula: p50 = 2 (generic pool + free list + reset hook) + 1 (wire the main effect-spawn path through it) + 1 (concurrency cap + oldest-recycling policy) + 1 (instrumentation: allocations/sec, peak occupancy) + 1 (soak test with burst spawning) = 6; p80 = p50 x ~2.3 (reset-completeness bugs and per-effect cap tuning dominate) = 14. Much lower if the engine already pools emitters.

dependencies: A single, central effect-spawn API (so pooling is not bypassed)
A concurrency cap policy per effect

relations.note: Fixed GPU allocation and CPU pooling solve allocation at two different layers; both are usually present.
Both are 'cap concurrency, recycle the oldest' budget policies applied to different object types.
Pooling removes spawn cost; atlases remove per-instance texture/binding cost. Together they make high effect density affordable.
Baked flipbook emitters are the cheapest pooled instances, so they are the natural bulk of a pool.

particle_pooling.verification: Run a 10-minute soak that spawns effects at 2-3x the design peak rate and record: allocations per second (assert ~0 after warm-up), peak pool occupancy, and the p99 frame time. Compare p99 frame time against a non-pooled build to quantify the spike reduction. Then deliberately exhaust the pool and assert the chosen exhaustion policy behaves (drops or recycles oldest) without stalling or leaking.

claims.statement: Game Programming Patterns documents the Object Pool pattern as a way to avoid allocation and fragmentation by reusing a fixed set of pre-allocated objects instead of creating and destroying them at runtime.

The Object Pool discussion's central design question is what happens when the pool is exhausted - refuse, grow, or recycle - i.e. pooling converts an allocation problem into a capacity-policy decision that must be made explicitly.
Godot's GPU particle system allocates for the declared total amount regardless of how many particles are actually alive, which structurally removes per-spawn allocation for the particles themselves.

Unreal's Significance Manager is documented as evaluating object significance so objects can modify behaviour 'by doing things like shutting off Components like Particle Emitters, or by running complex AI code less frequently'.

Unreal's documentation explicitly states the Significance Manager does not actually improve performance by itself - it is a framework for making degradation decisions, and the work must still be implemented per object type.
No published measurement of frame-spike reduction attributable specifically to particle pooling was found in the verified sources; the benefit must be measured on the target project.

game_examples.fact: The Object Pool pattern is documented as a standard optimisation pattern for games, motivated by memory fragmentation and allocation cost on consoles and in languages with garbage collection.
game_examples.non_transferable: This is a design-pattern reference, not evidence of a specific shipped game's results. It establishes that the technique is standard practice; it provides no measurement and no shipped-title confirmation.

sprite_particle_atlas.problem: A particle system that binds a different texture per effect (or per frame) pays state changes and draw-call setup, and cannot be batched. Packing all particle sprites into a single atlas (and driving variation via sub-UV) removes per-effect texture binding and lets many effects share one draw.

implementation_variants.name: Tiled atlas with sub-UV addressing (single texture, many sprite variants)
implementation_variants.description: The same mechanism that powers flipbooks: a tiled image where each tile is addressed by sub-UV. Epic's baker documentation shows the operational rules - tile count must divide evenly into the texture size, and the texture size should be a power of two, or the atlas jitters.

implementation_variants.name: Per-frame tiles for animation plus per-variant tiles for variation
implementation_variants.description: The atlas carries both the animation frames and the visual variants; the runtime selects a tile by frame index and variant. The Unreal example uses an 8x8 grid of 64 frames addressed 0-63 via the Sub UVAnimation module, with Sub Image Size on the Sprite Renderer.

implementation_variants.name: Material-side atlas sampling with premultiplied-alpha correction
implementation_variants.description: Epic's documented material setup for a flipbook/atlas: sample the atlas, then divide RGB by alpha to remove black premultiplication and avoid black fringing around sprites - a practical requirement for atlas edges, not an optional nicety.

implementation_variants.name: Engine-side batching of atlas-shared sprites
implementation_variants.description: The performance reason to atlas is batching: GPU instancing is the documented general mechanism for drawing many copies of the same mesh/material in one draw call, and atlasing is what makes many particle effects share one material. Verified only from the Unity GPU-instancing manual URL, which was reachable but content-blocked by a cookie/consent wall, so no content claim is made from it.

sprite_particle_atlas.applicability_conditions: Any project with many distinct small particle sprites. Strongest when the particle count is high and draw-call/binding overhead is a measured bottleneck. Requires that all sprites in an atlas share a material and blend mode (additive vs alpha-blended sprites should not share an atlas unless sorting is handled).
sprite_particle_atlas.limitations: All sprites in an atlas share one texture, so they share filtering, compression and mip behaviour - a high-frequency sprite forces the whole atlas to higher resolution. Mipmapping an atlas causes bleeding between tiles unless padding or per-tile mip handling is used. Blend modes and sorting constrain what can share an atlas. Changing one sprite forces a re-bake of the atlas.
sprite_particle_atlas.required_data_and_tools: An atlas packing tool with padding and power-of-two control; a material that samples sub-UV; a validation step asserting tile size divides texture size; an overdraw/quad-cost measurement; a draw-call counter to confirm the batching actually happened.

impact.cpu: low reduction (fewer state changes and draw submissions)
impact.gpu: low-medium reduction in draw/binding overhead; no reduction in fill/overdraw, which usually still dominates for particles
impact.ram: low
impact.vram: low-medium increase (one larger texture instead of many small ones, plus padding waste) - a deliberate trade
impact.network: none

sprite_particle_atlas.quality_impact: Neutral to slightly negative on individual sprite fidelity (shared filtering/compression, mip bleed risk); positive on the ability to have many simultaneous effect types without a draw-call cliff.
sprite_particle_atlas.concept_impact: None directly; it is enabling infrastructure that lets the art team use more distinct effects.

effort_person_days.formula: p50 = 2 (packing pipeline: padding, power-of-two, validation) + 2 (sub-UV material + premultiply correction) + 2 (convert existing effects to the atlas) + 1 (draw-call before/after measurement) = 7; p80 = p50 x ~2.3 (mip-bleed and blend-mode/sorting rework across effect library dominate) = 16.

dependencies: A sub-UV-capable sprite material
An atlas packing step in the content pipeline
Agreement on blend modes per atlas

relations.note: A flipbook is an atlas whose tiles are animation frames; the packing rules and the jitter failure mode are identical.
GPU simulation raises particle counts and makes per-effect binding cost material; atlasing removes it.
Pooling fixes spawn cost, atlasing fixes draw cost; high effect density needs both.
Both are batching-by-shared-texture strategies for large numbers of small, similar draws.

sprite_particle_atlas.verification: Count draw calls (and material/texture bind changes) in the heaviest VFX scene before and after atlassing, and assert the reduction is real. Then inspect atlased sprites at the smallest on-screen size and assert no bleeding between tiles at higher mip levels. Finally confirm the atlas VRAM total fits the VFX texture budget and that no atlas has non-dividing tile counts (the documented jitter cause).

claims.statement: Epic's baker documentation states the operational rules for tiled particle textures: the number of tiles must divide evenly into the overall texture size, and for ideal behaviour the texture size should be a power of two with a frames-per-dimension count that divides it evenly.

When tiles do not divide evenly into the texture, leftover padding makes the sub UV mapping slightly off and causes the atlas to jitter as it plays - a concrete, documented artefact of bad atlas sizing.
claims.locator: 'Adjust the Texture Size' section, worked example

claims.statement: Epic's material setup notes that baked atlas colour channels are premultiplied with black by default, and that a divide node removing this from the RGB channels is needed to avoid black fringing around sprites.
claims.locator: 'Adjust the Settings on the Sprite Renderer' step 06

claims.statement: Atlas frames are selected at runtime by a Sub UVAnimation module (start/end frame) plus Sub Image Size on the Sprite Renderer; the documented example is an 8x8 grid giving 64 frames indexed 0 to 63.
claims.locator: 'Add the Sub UV Animation Module'; 'Adjust the Settings on the Sprite Renderer' step 01

claims.statement: The general batching motivation for atlases (sharing one material so many sprites draw in one call via GPU instancing) was not verified from primary documentation: the Unity GPU-instancing manual URL was reachable but returned only a cookie/consent shell, so no content claim is made from it. This is an explicitly unverified part of the method.
No published draw-call or millisecond saving for particle atlasing was found in the verified sources; the benefit must be measured per project with a draw-call counter.
claims.locator: page is a workflow guide, no measurements

game_examples.game: Unreal Engine Niagara sprite renderer (engine capability)
game_examples.fact: Unreal's Sprite Renderer exposes Sub Image Size and works with a Sub UVAnimation module, i.e. the engine has first-class support for tiled particle atlases and documents the correct sizing rules.
game_examples.locator: 'Use the Flipbook Texture in an Emitter' and 'Adjust the Texture Size'
game_examples.non_transferable: Engine capability, not a shipped-game result. No draw-call count, saving, or visual outcome transfers.

broadphase_spatial_partitioning.problem: Naive collision detection is O(n^2) pair tests. A broadphase rejects the vast majority of pairs cheaply before narrow-phase tests, and is the single biggest lever on physics cost as body count grows.

implementation_variants.name: Sweep-and-prune variants (PhysX eSAP, eABP, ePABP)
implementation_variants.description: PhysX documents several broadphase types: eSAP (sweep-and-prune, the default in some configurations), eABP (automated broadphase / parallel SAP), and ePABP (parallel auto broadphase), each with different scaling and parallelism characteristics, plus eMBP (multibox pruning) and eGPU.

implementation_variants.name: Grid/multibox pruning (PhysX eMBP)
implementation_variants.description: Multibox pruning is a grid-based broadphase that PhysX documents as an alternative to SAP; it suits large worlds with many bodies where a single sorted sweep is inefficient.

implementation_variants.name: GPU broadphase (PhysX eGPU / CUDA broad-phase)
implementation_variants.description: GPU Gems 3 Chapter 32 documents a CUDA broad-phase collision detection implementation, and reports sweeping 30,720 objects at roughly 79 fps with about a 26x speedup over the comparison, peaking at 487 fps at 3,072 objects.

implementation_variants.name: Layer/filter-level rejection before the broadphase
implementation_variants.description: Pair rejection by collision layer/mask is cheaper than any spatial structure and should be applied first; Godot exposes 32 physics layers and separate layer/mask bitmasks on every collision object.

broadphase_spatial_partitioning.applicability_conditions: Any scene with more than a few dozen dynamic bodies. Choice of algorithm depends on world size, body distribution (clustered vs uniform), and whether bodies are mostly static. Required for destruction with many fragments, for large prop counts, and for any physics-heavy simulation.
broadphase_spatial_partitioning.limitations: No single broadphase is optimal: SAP degrades with many objects spread on one axis; grid methods waste memory on sparse worlds and need tuning of cell size; GPU broadphase needs a capable GPU and adds readback/latency considerations. Broadphase only reduces pair tests - it does not help if the remaining pairs are genuinely all overlapping. Large worlds also need broadphase regions/streaming, which is a separate concern.
broadphase_spatial_partitioning.required_data_and_tools: A physics SDK exposing a selectable broadphase (PhysX, Bullet, Havok, or in-house); a pair-count and broadphase-time readout; a profiler; a stress scene with a realistic body distribution (not a uniform grid) and a degenerate case (all bodies stacked in one place).

impact.cpu: high leverage: broadphase time typically dominates physics time at high body counts; the GPU Gems 3 CUDA implementation reports roughly 26x speedup and ~79 fps at 30,720 objects versus its CPU comparison
impact.gpu: none for CPU variants; medium if the GPU broadphase is used (and it competes with rendering for GPU time)
impact.ram: low-medium (the broadphase structure; grid methods scale with world volume and cell size)
impact.network: none

broadphase_spatial_partitioning.quality_impact: Indirect but decisive: a bad broadphase caps how many physical objects the game can have, which caps destruction, props and debris. It does not change how physics looks.
broadphase_spatial_partitioning.concept_impact: Determines whether physics-dense design (destruction, debris, physics puzzles, large prop counts) is feasible at all.

effort_person_days.formula: p50 = 1 (select broadphase type in the SDK) + 2 (stress scene with realistic body distribution + pair-count instrumentation) + 1 (tune parameters: cell size / world bounds / region count) + 1 (validate degenerate stacking case) = 5; p80 = p50 x ~2.4 (clustered-world and streaming edge cases dominate; much higher if a custom broadphase is written) = 12. Excludes writing a broadphase from scratch (add 15-30).

dependencies: A physics SDK with a selectable broadphase
Instrumentation exposing broadphase time and pair counts

relations.note: Layer/mask filtering is cheaper than spatial rejection and runs first; the two stack.
Parallelising physics only pays if the broadphase itself scales; PhysX exposes parallel SAP variants for exactly this reason.
Sleeping removes bodies from the active set, which is the cheapest possible broadphase win.
Destruction produces bursts of thousands of small bodies in one region - the worst case for most broadphases and the reason fragment caps exist.

broadphase_spatial_partitioning.verification: Build a stress scene with the maximum expected dynamic body count in a realistic distribution and record broadphase time, narrowphase time and pair count separately. Sweep the available broadphase types (SAP / MBP / ABP / GPU) and pick the best empirically rather than by reputation. Then run the degenerate case (all bodies in one small volume) and assert no superlinear blowup. Re-run whenever body-count targets change.

claims.statement: PhysX exposes multiple broadphase algorithms through PxBroadPhaseType, including sweep-and-prune variants (eSAP, eABP, ePABP), multibox pruning (eMBP), and a GPU broadphase (eGPU) - i.e. broadphase choice is an exposed, tunable engine parameter rather than a fixed implementation.
claims.locator: PxBroadPhaseType enum members (eSAP, eMBP, eABP, ePABP, eGPU)

claims.statement: GPU Gems 3 Chapter 32 (Broad-Phase Collision Detection with CUDA) reports its CUDA broad-phase handling 30,720 objects at roughly 79 fps.
GPU Gems 3 Chapter 32 reports about a 26x speedup for its CUDA broad-phase versus the compared implementation, peaking at 487 fps at 3,072 objects.

The GPU Gems 3 figures are from a 2007-era CUDA research chapter on a specific GPU and a synthetic benchmark; they demonstrate the scaling potential of a GPU broadphase but are not a current hardware measurement and must not be quoted as a shipped-game result.
Godot exposes 32 physics layers for 3D, with separate layer and mask bitmasks on collision objects, giving a cheap pre-broadphase rejection mechanism.
No current-generation published comparison of PhysX broadphase types on a specified CPU/GPU was found; the choice must be made by measurement on the target project's own body distribution.
claims.locator: enum reference page - describes types, no benchmarks

game_examples.engine: PhysX SDK (used by Unreal, Unity and many in-house engines)
game_examples.fact: PhysX exposes an explicitly selectable broadphase (sweep-and-prune, multibox pruning, parallel variants, and a GPU broadphase), so broadphase selection is a documented, tunable production decision in shipped engines.
game_examples.non_transferable: Confirms the mechanism is exposed in shipping middleware, not that any particular game chose any particular type. No game-specific body counts or timings transfer.

collision_layer_matrix.problem: Without filtering, the physics system tests (and reports) collisions between objects that can never meaningfully interact: debris against debris, player triggers against other triggers, camera blockers against projectiles. A layer/mask matrix rejects these pairs before any geometric work and is the cheapest possible collision optimisation.

implementation_variants.name: Layer bitmask + mask bitmask per object (Godot model)
implementation_variants.description: Each collision object declares which physics layers it is on (collision_layer) and which layers it scans (collision_mask); a pair is considered only if the layer of each is in the mask of the other. Godot exposes 32 layers for 3D.

implementation_variants.name: Engine collision presets / profile matrix (Unreal model)
implementation_variants.description: Unreal documents collision presets and collision responses as a first-class concept with a dedicated collision documentation section - equivalent filtering expressed as named presets rather than raw bitmasks.

implementation_variants.name: Object-channel + trace-channel split (query vs simulation filtering)
implementation_variants.description: Filtering has to be defined separately for simulation (what collides) and for queries (what raycasts/traces hit); Unreal's physics documentation separates 'Collision' from 'Traces with Raycasts' as distinct topics, reflecting that these are separate matrices in practice.

implementation_variants.name: Layer matrix as a designed, documented artefact, reviewed like code
implementation_variants.description: In practice the matrix is written down as a table and reviewed, because a wrong bit silently removes gameplay collisions. The specific layer taxonomy is project-specific and is expert_estimate here; only the mechanism is documented.

collision_layer_matrix.applicability_conditions: Any project using a physics engine. Mandatory once there are multiple object categories (player, enemy, projectile, trigger, debris, camera, ragdoll, vehicle). Should be designed early, because retrofitting a layer taxonomy means auditing every existing object.
collision_layer_matrix.limitations: A layer bit set wrongly is a silent bug: two things simply stop colliding and no error is raised. Limited layer count (Godot: 32) forces grouping that can be too coarse for complex projects. Layers do not express conditional filtering (e.g. 'ignore this collision only for 0.2 s after spawn'), which must be handled by other mechanisms. Query and simulation filtering are separate and are commonly confused.
collision_layer_matrix.required_data_and_tools: A documented layer taxonomy table; a way to audit which objects are on which layer; a debug visualisation that renders only a given layer; regression tests asserting key gameplay collisions still occur (projectile hits enemy, player stands on floor).

impact.cpu: low-medium but very cheap to obtain: removes pair tests before the broadphase and removes unwanted collision events from gameplay code
impact.gpu: none
impact.ram: negligible (two bitmask words per object)
impact.network: none

collision_layer_matrix.quality_impact: Neutral when correct, severe when wrong: missed collisions read as bugs (shots passing through, falling through floors), and spurious collisions read as jank (invisible walls, camera snagging).
collision_layer_matrix.concept_impact: None directly; it is hygiene that protects every physics-dependent feature.

effort_person_days.formula: p50 = 1 (define layer taxonomy table) + 1 (assign layers to existing object types) + 1 (regression tests for key collision pairs) + 1 (debug visualisation by layer) = 4; p80 = p50 x 2.5 (retrofitting a taxonomy onto an existing, grown content base is where the cost actually lands) = 10.

dependencies: A physics engine exposing layer/mask or collision presets
An agreed object-category taxonomy

relations.note: Layer filtering runs before spatial rejection and is cheaper; the two are complementary and both should be used.
Sleeping and layer filtering are both ways of removing pairs from the simulation, and both need care to not remove gameplay-relevant pairs.
Debris should generally not collide with debris; a layer bit is the cheapest way to make that true.
Both are filtering systems where a wrongly set bit silently removes behaviour with no error.

collision_layer_matrix.verification: Write automated assertions for every gameplay-critical collision pair (projectile-enemy, player-floor, vehicle-barrier, trigger-player) and run them in CI, so a changed layer bit fails a test rather than shipping. Then count candidate pairs before and after the matrix is applied in the heaviest scene and record the reduction. Finally, add a debug mode that renders only one layer at a time to make mis-assignment visible.

claims.statement: Godot gives every collision object a collision_layer (which layers it is on) and a collision_mask (which layers it scans), so a pair is only tested when each object's layer is inside the other's mask.
Godot exposes 32 physics layers in 3D, which bounds how fine-grained a layer taxonomy can be.

Unreal's physics documentation treats 'Collision' and 'Traces with Raycasts' as separate documentation topics, reflecting that simulation filtering and query filtering are configured separately in practice.
Unreal documents collision responses and collision presets as named, reusable configurations rather than requiring raw bitmask entry per object.
No published measurement of pair-count reduction attributable to a layer matrix was found in the verified sources; the reduction must be measured on the project's own scenes.

game_examples.fact: Godot exposes 32 physics layers with per-object layer and mask bitmasks as the standard, documented mechanism for filtering both collision simulation and queries.
game_examples.non_transferable: Engine capability, not a shipped-game result. No pair counts, timings, or layer taxonomy transfers to another project or engine.

fixed_timestep_physics.problem: Physics integration is only stable and reproducible at a fixed, small timestep. Driving it from a variable frame delta makes simulation behaviour depend on framerate: stacks jitter, joints stretch, vehicles handle differently when the frame rate drops, and results are not reproducible for replays or networking.

implementation_variants.name: Fixed timestep with accumulator and interpolated rendering (canonical)
implementation_variants.description: Gaffer on Games' 'Fix Your Timestep!' is the canonical engineering write-up: accumulate real time, consume it in fixed dt steps, and render with an interpolated remainder so motion stays smooth. It explicitly argues against feeding a variable delta to the integrator and against the 'semi-fixed' compromise.

implementation_variants.name: Engine default fixed tick (Godot: 60 Hz physics default)
implementation_variants.description: Godot's physics introduction documents a default physics tick rate of 60 Hz, i.e. the physics tick is decoupled from render framerate by default rather than by choice.

implementation_variants.name: Sub-stepping as a variable-framerate compensation layer (Unreal)
implementation_variants.description: Unreal documents sub-stepping as taking the total frame time and dividing it into sub-steps, ticking physics multiple times per frame, with Max Substep Delta Time and Max Substeps as controls (worked example: 0.05 s full step with 0.025 s max substep splits into 2 sub-steps, and Max Physics Delta Time limits how long a step may take). Epic states this improves accuracy and stability 'at the expense of performance', and that forces applied for one frame must be applied across all sub-steps.

implementation_variants.name: Clamped maximum step to avoid the spiral of death
implementation_variants.description: A cap on how much time a single frame may feed the simulation (Unreal's Max Physics Delta Time; the 'spiral of death' in the Fix Your Timestep write-up) prevents a slow frame from generating more simulation work, which generates a slower frame.

fixed_timestep_physics.applicability_conditions: Required for any project with joints, stacks, vehicles, ragdolls, cloth or any stability-sensitive simulation. Mandatory for deterministic replay, lockstep networking, or physics-based gameplay that must feel identical across hardware. Should be decided at prototype stage, because simulation tuning done against a variable timestep has to be redone.
fixed_timestep_physics.limitations: A fixed step at a low rate (e.g. 30 Hz) degrades fast-moving collision response unless CCD or substepping is used. Very small steps cost CPU linearly. Sub-stepping changes callback semantics: Unreal warns that collision callbacks are delayed until the final sub-step, so you can receive both an overlap and an end-overlap for the same pair in one frame. Sub-stepping is documented as not supported on mobile and not fully supported by APEX Destruction. Interpolated rendering adds one frame of latency to physics-driven visuals.
fixed_timestep_physics.required_data_and_tools: A game loop with an accumulator; profiler hooks separating physics tick from render; a deterministic replay harness (record inputs, replay, compare final transforms); a test scene with stacks, joints and a fast projectile; a timescale control for debugging.

impact.cpu: low-medium and bounded: cost becomes proportional to the number of fixed steps per frame, so a slow frame costs more steps unless clamped (hence the max-step cap)
impact.gpu: none directly
impact.ram: low (one or two transform snapshots for interpolation)
impact.network: strongly beneficial: a fixed step is a prerequisite for deterministic or server-authoritative physics

fixed_timestep_physics.quality_impact: Removes framerate-dependent feel - a vehicle handles the same at 40 and 120 fps. Removes stack jitter and joint stretch. Invisible when correct; pervasive and obvious when wrong.
fixed_timestep_physics.concept_impact: Unlocks any design that depends on reproducible physics (skill-based driving, physics puzzles, determinstic replay, server-authoritative simulation).

effort_person_days.formula: p50 = 2 (accumulator loop + clamp) + 1 (render interpolation of physics transforms) + 1 (determinism replay harness) + 1 (retune existing simulation constants for the fixed rate) = 5; p80 = p50 x ~2.4 (retuning springs/damping/joints that were tuned against a variable delta, plus substep callback rework, dominate) = 12. Lower if the engine already ships a fixed tick.

dependencies: A game loop you control (or an engine exposing the physics tick rate)
Render interpolation for physics-driven transforms

relations.note: A fixed step makes the physics tick a predictable unit of work, which is what makes it schedulable and async-safe.
Spring-based cloth stretches and explodes under variable deltas; it needs a stable step.
Suspension feel is timestep-dependent; without a fixed step, handling changes with framerate.
A cache baked at one timestep and replayed at another will pop or drift; bake and runtime must agree.

fixed_timestep_physics.verification: Run the same scripted input sequence at 30, 60 and 144 fps and assert final transforms agree within a tight epsilon (or exactly, if determinism is a requirement). Then measure physics tick count per frame under a deliberately overloaded frame and assert the max-step clamp prevents the step count from exploding. Finally, sweep the fixed rate (e.g. 30/50/60/120 Hz) and record both CPU cost and stack/joint stability to pick the rate empirically.

claims.statement: The 'Fix Your Timestep!' engineering write-up is the canonical reference for decoupling physics from render framerate using a fixed timestep with an accumulator, and explicitly argues against passing a variable delta to the integrator.
Godot's physics introduction documents a default physics tick rate of 60 Hz, i.e. a fixed physics tick separated from render framerate by default.
Unreal states that Unreal Engine 5 uses a variable frame rate, that this is good for hardware scalability but creates a challenge for the physics engine, which works best with small fixed time steps.

Unreal states that sub-stepping gives more accurate and stable simulation 'however, this comes at the expense of performance', and that the smaller the max sub-step time the more stable the simulation but at greater CPU cost.

Unreal's documented worked example: if a full step takes 0.05 s and Max Substep Delta Time is 0.025, the full step is split into 2 sub-steps; if a step took 2 s it would be split by Max Substeps rather than into 80 steps, and Max Physics Delta Time limits how long a physics step is permitted to take.

Unreal warns that with sub-stepping, collision callbacks are delayed until the final sub-step so you can get several callbacks for the same collision - for example both an overlap and an end-overlap for A and B in the same frame - and that callbacks are queued so sub-step 1 is processed before sub-step 2.
Unreal states sub-stepping is still a work in progress, is not fully supported by APEX Destruction, and is not currently supported on mobile devices.

game_examples.fact: The SIGGRAPH 2020 presentation states the game holds 60 FPS on consoles, and its results section reports up to 5 ms of GPU savings in dense scenes from triangle culling and merging - evidence of an explicit, measured frame budget culture rather than a physics-timestep claim.
game_examples.locator: PDF p.4 ('Still 60FPS on consoles at same resolutions') and p.53 ('RESULTS - Up to 5ms GPU savings in dense scenes with triangle culling+merging')
game_examples.non_transferable: The 5 ms figure is for triangle culling/merging, not for physics timestep, and the 60 FPS target is that game's own target on its own hardware. Neither number transfers to another project; the transferable observation is that a shipped AAA title publishes and holds an explicit frame budget.

multithreaded_physics_jobs.problem: Physics is one of the last big serial blocks in a frame. Running collision detection, solving and integration across worker threads (or off the game thread entirely) removes it from the critical path, but requires the simulation to be isolated from gameplay state and introduces a frame of latency and synchronisation complexity.

implementation_variants.name: Asynchronous physics simulation off the game thread (Unreal Chaos)
implementation_variants.description: Unreal documents asynchronous physics simulation as a feature of Chaos rigid-body dynamics, and notes that physics sub-stepping runs in a separate physics thread allowing the game thread to continue doing work.

implementation_variants.name: Async physics mode for determinism, not only throughput
implementation_variants.description: Unreal documents that Chaos Vehicles support the Asynchronous Physics mode in Unreal Engine 5, which 'improves the determinism of the simulation and allows for predictable results every time the simulation runs' - i.e. the async mode is sold on determinism, not just parallelism.

implementation_variants.name: Data-oriented parallel jobs over component arrays (Unity DOTS)
implementation_variants.description: Unity's DOTS stack is the vendor product page for a data-oriented, job-system-based approach where work is expressed as parallel jobs over component arrays. Verified only as a vendor product page; no benchmark was retrieved from it.

implementation_variants.name: Parallel broadphase as the first parallelisation target
implementation_variants.description: PhysX exposes explicitly parallel broadphase variants (automated/parallel SAP), i.e. the vendor's own answer to scaling the part of physics that dominates at high body counts.

multithreaded_physics_jobs.applicability_conditions: Worth doing when physics is a measured significant fraction of the frame and the simulation can be isolated from gameplay reads/writes for a tick. Requires an engine with a job system or an async physics mode. Most valuable with high body counts (destruction, debris, vehicles, crowds of physical props).
multithreaded_physics_jobs.limitations: Async physics means gameplay typically reads last frame's physics state, adding latency that must be hidden or accepted. Callbacks arrive on a different thread or are deferred, which complicates gameplay code that expects to react immediately. Jobified physics requires data to be laid out for parallel access, which usually means an ECS- or array-oriented refactor. It does not reduce total work, only wall-clock; on a single-core-bound platform it can be a net loss.
multithreaded_physics_jobs.required_data_and_tools: An engine job system or async physics mode; a profiler showing the physics thread against the game thread; a synchronisation/latency measurement; a soak test exercising maximum body count; a determinism harness if determinism is claimed.

impact.cpu: medium-high reduction in main-thread physics time; total CPU work is unchanged or slightly higher (scheduling, copying, sync)
impact.gpu: none (PhysX exposes a GPU broadphase/rigid-body path as a separate, optional choice)
impact.ram: low-medium (double-buffered state for the async handoff)
impact.network: indirectly beneficial via determinism; networked physics is a separate documented feature

multithreaded_physics_jobs.quality_impact: No visual change. The risk is latency and jitter: if gameplay reads stale physics state without interpolation, motion looks rubbery or input feels late.
multithreaded_physics_jobs.concept_impact: Raises the ceiling on how many physical objects a design can assume, which can unlock destruction- and debris-heavy design.

effort_person_days.formula: p50 = 2 (enable async/jobified physics) + 3 (audit and fix gameplay reads/writes that assumed synchronous physics) + 3 (callback deferral and thread-safety work) + 2 (latency measurement + interpolation where needed) + 2 (soak + determinism check) = 12; p80 = p50 x ~2.3 (the audit of gameplay code that assumed synchronous physics is unbounded and dominates) = 28. Excludes a data-oriented refactor of gameplay (which is the composition_bootstrap_architecture / ECS project).

dependencies: An engine with a job system or async physics mode
A fixed physics timestep (so the work is a predictable unit)
Gameplay code that does not assume synchronous physics results

relations.note: A predictable fixed step is what makes the physics tick schedulable and safe to run off-thread.
Parallelising only pays if the broadphase itself scales; PhysX ships parallel broadphase variants for this reason.
Both require data laid out for parallel access; the refactor is largely the same work.
Sleeping shrinks the parallel workload, so it still pays even after jobification.

multithreaded_physics_jobs.verification: Profile the frame and assert main-thread physics time drops by the expected amount while total physics work (all threads) does not increase materially. Then measure the latency between a gameplay input and the physics response and assert it is within the design's tolerance. Finally run a 10-minute soak at maximum body count and assert no race-induced nondeterminism (compare final transforms across runs) if determinism is required.

claims.statement: Unreal documents that Chaos rigid-body dynamics provides asynchronous physics simulation as a feature.
Unreal states it runs physics sub-stepping in a separate physics thread, allowing the game thread to continue doing work.

Unreal documents that Chaos Vehicles support the Asynchronous Physics mode in Unreal Engine 5, which improves the determinism of the simulation and allows predictable results every time the simulation runs.

Unreal treats networked physics as part of the networking framework enabling physics-driven simulations to work in multiplayer - i.e. it is a distinct feature from async physics and does not come for free with it.
PhysX exposes parallel broadphase variants (automated broadphase and parallel auto broadphase) alongside the classic sweep-and-prune, so the broadphase is explicitly designed for parallel scaling.

Unity's DOTS product page was verified as reachable but it is a marketing/product page; no benchmark or measured throughput figure was retrieved from it, so no performance claim is made for DOTS here.

The Unity job system manual page (https://docs.unity3d.com/Manual/JobSystem.html) was reachable but returned only client-rendered chrome with no retrievable content, so no content claim about Unity's job system is made in this pack.

game_examples.game: Unreal Engine 5 titles using Chaos Vehicles
game_examples.fact: Unreal documents that Chaos Vehicles support the engine's Asynchronous Physics mode, and markets it primarily as improving determinism and predictability rather than raw throughput.
game_examples.non_transferable: Engine capability, not a shipped-game result. No measured speedup, thread count, or body count transfers, and the determinism benefit is a property of that engine mode, not of async physics in general.

physics_lod_sleeping.problem: Most dynamic bodies in a level are at rest most of the time, but a naive simulation integrates and solves all of them every tick. Deactivation ('sleeping') removes resting bodies from the solve, and LOD policies reduce or disable simulation for distant or insignificant objects.

implementation_variants.name: Per-body sleep with automatic wake on contact or impulse (Godot model)
implementation_variants.description: A body with can_sleep enabled enters sleep mode when there is no movement; a sleeping body 'will not move and will not calculate forces until woken up by another body through, for example, a collision, or by using the apply_impulse() or apply_force() methods', and emits sleeping_state_changed when the engine changes the state.

implementation_variants.name: Significance-driven simulation LOD (Unreal Significance Manager)
implementation_variants.description: Rather than a per-body heuristic, evaluate significance and let objects degrade: the manager exists so objects can 'modify their behavior by doing things like shutting off Components like Particle Emitters, or by running complex AI code less frequently'. Epic explicitly notes the manager 'does not actually improve performance' by itself - it is the decision framework, not the optimisation.

implementation_variants.name: Per-body-type budget with thread-safety requirement
implementation_variants.description: Unreal's Significance Manager documentation describes per-Actor-type significance evaluation and requires the registered callbacks to be thread-safe, i.e. this is infrastructure with real integration constraints rather than a checkbox.

implementation_variants.name: Distance/dormancy policies for streaming worlds
implementation_variants.description: Combine sleeping with a distance policy so bodies outside the active region are not simulated at all. The specific thresholds are project parameters and are expert_estimate here; what is documented is only the per-body sleep mechanism and the significance framework.

physics_lod_sleeping.applicability_conditions: Any project with more dynamic bodies than are simultaneously active - which is nearly every project. Essential for levels with many props, for destruction debris, and for open worlds. Effectiveness depends on the ratio of resting to moving bodies: a level where everything is permanently in motion gains little.
physics_lod_sleeping.limitations: Sleeping bodies will not respond to changes that do not go through the documented wake paths - moving the world, changing gravity, or teleporting an object onto a sleeping body may fail to wake it (which is why the API exposes explicit wake/apply_force/apply_impulse). Sleep thresholds are tuned per project and a badly tuned threshold causes visible premature parking or a body that never sleeps. Sleeping interacts badly with gameplay that queries physics state, because a sleeping body reports stale or zero velocity. It does not help if the design genuinely keeps everything moving.
physics_lod_sleeping.required_data_and_tools: A sleep API with explicit wake control; a readout of active vs sleeping body count; a debug renderer colouring bodies by state; a soak test that lets a busy scene come to rest and asserts the active count approaches zero; a regression test that asserts gameplay-critical bodies (platforms, doors) are never parked.

impact.cpu: high leverage in prop-heavy scenes: the saving is proportional to the fraction of bodies at rest, and it is the cheapest physics win available
impact.gpu: none (a sleeping body still renders; it just is not simulated)
impact.ram: low (a state bit per body, plus whatever the significance framework keeps)
impact.network: none directly; a sleeping body's state may need explicit replication if it matters

physics_lod_sleeping.quality_impact: Invisible when correct. Failure modes are visible and bad: props that fail to wake when shot, platforms that stop moving, bodies that visibly freeze mid-fall.
physics_lod_sleeping.concept_impact: Determines the affordable prop and debris density of a level, and therefore how physical the world can feel.

effort_person_days.formula: p50 = 1 (enable/verify sleep) + 2 (active-vs-sleeping instrumentation + debug colouring) + 1 (wake-path audit: ensure gameplay forces use impulse/force or explicit wake) + 1 (significance policy for one object class) + 1 (soak test asserting active count decays) = 6; p80 = p50 x ~2.3 (wake-path bugs - things that fail to wake - dominate and are discovered late) = 14.

dependencies: A physics engine with a sleep/deactivation mechanism
Instrumentation exposing active vs sleeping body counts

relations.note: Sleeping removes bodies from the active set, which is strictly cheaper than rejecting them in the broadphase.
Both remove pairs from the simulation; both fail silently when misconfigured.
Significance-driven LOD is the same policy engine applied to AI rather than to rigid bodies.
Debris that never sleeps will consume the entire destruction budget; sleeping is what makes debris affordable.

physics_lod_sleeping.verification: Let a busy scene come to rest and assert the active body count decays to near zero (and that it does so within the expected settle time). Then attack: shoot, push and teleport objects onto sleeping bodies and assert each wakes correctly. Finally measure physics tick time with and without sleeping in the same scene and record the delta - this is the actual win and it is project-specific.

claims.statement: In Godot, if can_sleep is true a body can enter sleep mode when there is no movement.
A sleeping Godot body 'will not move and will not calculate forces until woken up by another body through, for example, a collision, or by using the apply_impulse() or apply_force() methods'.
Godot emits sleeping_state_changed when the physics engine changes a body's sleeping state, and notes that setting the sleeping property directly will not trigger the signal.

Unreal's Significance Manager is documented as a framework for evaluating object significance so objects can modify their behaviour 'by doing things like shutting off Components like Particle Emitters, or by running complex AI code less frequently'.

Unreal's documentation explicitly states the Significance Manager does not actually improve performance by itself - it provides the significance evaluation; the actual degradation work must be implemented.

Unreal's Significance Manager documentation describes per-Actor-type significance evaluation and requires thread-safe handling, i.e. integrating it is real work with concurrency constraints, not a toggle.
No published measurement of the physics-time saving from sleeping was found in the verified sources; the saving depends entirely on the resting-to-moving body ratio in the project's own scenes.
claims.locator: class reference - mechanism only, no benchmarks

game_examples.fact: Sleeping is on by default (can_sleep defaults to true) with documented wake paths via collision, apply_impulse and apply_force, and a sleeping_state_changed signal for reacting to state changes.
game_examples.non_transferable: Engine capability, not a shipped-game result. No body counts, settle times or savings transfer; threshold tuning is project-specific.

composition_bootstrap_architecture.problem: Deep inheritance hierarchies for gameplay entities produce rigid, unmaintainable code: a change to a base class affects everything, and combining behaviours (flying + explosive + carryable) is impossible without combinatorial subclasses. Composition - entities as containers of components with a bootstrapping layer that wires them - is the standard alternative.

implementation_variants.name: Component pattern: entity as a container of loosely-coupled components
implementation_variants.description: Game Programming Patterns' Component chapter documents the canonical solution: decompose a monolithic entity class into collaborating components, with the entity reduced to identity plus a component list. It gives the explicit trade-off that components add indirection and that cross-component communication becomes a design problem.

implementation_variants.name: Engine-provided Actor/Component model with a bootstrapping pass
implementation_variants.description: Unreal's gameplay framework is Actor/Component based, so the bootstrapping question becomes 'who creates and wires the components, and in what order' rather than 'should we use components'. This is the common shipped shape.

implementation_variants.name: ECS / data-oriented composition (archetypes of components in arrays)
implementation_variants.description: Unity DOTS (vendor product page) and Unreal MassEntity (documentation index) are the shipped engine examples of moving composition from object graphs to arrays of components grouped by archetype, which is what makes the same composition model parallelisable.

implementation_variants.name: Overwatch's component-based entity administration
implementation_variants.description: Blizzard's GDC 2017 talk on Overwatch's gameplay architecture and netcode documents the component-based entity administration used on a shipped, networked, ability-heavy game - the highest-value single reference for composition at scale with networking.

composition_bootstrap_architecture.applicability_conditions: Any project with more than a handful of entity types, especially where behaviours must be recombined (abilities, status effects, vehicle/character hybrids). Decided at preproduction/prototype, because it is the decision that is most expensive to reverse later. Less critical for small or highly linear games.
composition_bootstrap_architecture.limitations: Composition moves complexity from the class hierarchy into wiring and ordering: who creates components, in what order, and how they find each other. Cross-component communication needs an explicit mechanism (events, shared data, direct references) and each has failure modes. Indirection costs some performance versus hard-coded members. Done badly it becomes 'everything is a component', which is harder to read than the hierarchy it replaced.
composition_bootstrap_architecture.required_data_and_tools: A component/entity model (engine-provided or in-house); an explicit bootstrapping and initialisation-order definition; a data-driven way to define entity templates/prefabs/archetypes; debug tooling to inspect an entity's component set at runtime; a convention for cross-component communication.

impact.cpu: low-medium: indirection costs some time; the ECS variants trade that back by improving cache locality. Direction depends on which variant is chosen.
impact.gpu: none
impact.ram: low-medium: object-graph composition has per-component overhead; ECS variants are tighter but add archetype bookkeeping
impact.network: composition strongly affects replication design: what is replicated is usually per-component or per-entity-state, so the choice determines how hard netcode is

composition_bootstrap_architecture.quality_impact: No direct visual impact. It determines how fast the team can add and recombine features, which is the dominant quality factor over a production cycle.
composition_bootstrap_architecture.concept_impact: High: composition is what makes emergent-combination design (abilities, status effects, modular vehicles, modular enemies) tractable. Without it, designers get only the combinations that were hard-coded.

effort_person_days.formula: p50 = 3 (define entity/component model and ownership rules) + 2 (bootstrap/initialisation-order pass) + 2 (data-driven entity templates for one content area) + 2 (cross-component communication convention + debug inspector) + 1 (migrate one representative entity as a template) = 10; p80 = p50 x 2.5 (migration of existing entities and ordering bugs dominate) = 25. Moving to full ECS multiplies this several times and is a separate project.

dependencies: An agreed entity/component model before content production begins
A data-driven way to author entity definitions

relations.note: A full ECS/data-oriented architecture is the same composition decision taken to its performance-oriented conclusion; you cannot adopt the crowd approach without the architectural one.
Jobified physics needs data laid out for parallel access, which the ECS variant of composition provides.

async_incremental_saves.problem: Serialising game state is I/O- and CPU-heavy and typically happens at the worst moment (checkpoint, quit, autosave). A synchronous save produces a visible hitch; a monolithic save rewrites the whole world state every time even when almost nothing changed.

implementation_variants.name: Asynchronous save API as the recommended path (Unreal)
implementation_variants.description: Unreal's saving documentation recommends the async save path (AsyncSaveGameToSlot) and notes that the synchronous path is 'sufficient for small SaveGame formats' - i.e. sync vs async is framed as a function of save size.

implementation_variants.name: Smaller serialisation format first (binary over JSON)
implementation_variants.description: Godot's saving documentation states binary serialization should produce smaller files than JSON, handles most common data types, and requires less custom encoding/decoding logic - i.e. format choice is the first lever before threading.

implementation_variants.name: Incremental / staged writes of nested object graphs
implementation_variants.description: Godot's documentation notes that nested persistent objects must be saved in stages (parents first, then children) because NodePaths would otherwise be invalid, i.e. save is naturally a staged operation - the same decomposition an incremental save uses.

implementation_variants.name: Serialisation by declared storage usage flag
implementation_variants.description: Godot documents that only properties configured with the PROPERTY_USAGE_STORAGE flag are serialised, which is the mechanism by which a project controls exactly what - and therefore how much - gets written.

async_incremental_saves.applicability_conditions: Any project with save games. Async is required once the serialised size is large enough that writing it produces a visible hitch. Incremental writes matter for open-world or persistent-world games where total state is large but per-checkpoint delta is small. Choose the format early: retrofitting a binary format breaks existing saves.
async_incremental_saves.limitations: An async save means the game keeps running while the snapshot is being taken, so the serialised state must be a consistent snapshot - otherwise you save a world that is half-updated. This usually requires double-buffering or a copy-on-write snapshot, which costs memory. Incremental saves complicate load (must reconcile deltas) and make corruption harder to detect and recover from. Save format versioning is required from day one or old saves break.
async_incremental_saves.required_data_and_tools: An async file I/O path; a serialisation format with versioning; a consistent-snapshot mechanism (double buffer or copy-on-write); measurement of save size and save duration; a corruption/recovery test (truncate a save file and assert graceful failure); a user-facing policy for what happens if the game is quit mid-save.

impact.cpu: medium burst moved off the critical path; async converts a hitch into background work, it does not remove the work
impact.gpu: none
impact.ram: medium transient (the snapshot buffer); this is the real cost of async saving
impact.disk: medium-high (save file size); binary formats are documented as smaller than JSON
impact.network: none for local saves; cloud saves add upload and conflict handling

async_incremental_saves.quality_impact: Directly felt: an autosave hitch at a checkpoint is one of the most noticed technical faults in a game. Done well, saving is invisible.
async_incremental_saves.concept_impact: Determines whether frequent autosaving (and therefore low-penalty death/retry design) is acceptable. A game with a 2-second save hitch cannot autosave aggressively.

effort_person_days.formula: p50 = 2 (async save path + completion callback) + 2 (consistent-snapshot mechanism) + 2 (versioned serialisation format) + 2 (instrumentation: save size, save duration, hitch measurement) + 1 (corruption/recovery test) = 9; p80 = p50 x ~2.2 (snapshot-consistency bugs - half-updated saves - and format migration dominate) = 20. Excludes cloud-save conflict resolution.

A way to take a consistent snapshot of mutable game state
An async file I/O path

Then serialise-during-mutation: force an autosave while the world is actively changing and verify the loaded save is internally consistent (no half-updated object graphs). Finally, measure save file size and duration against a budget, and test truncated/corrupted save files for graceful failure.
