snapshot_slot_saves.problem: A save system must decide what a 'save' is. The snapshot-in-a-slot model writes a complete, self-contained serialisation of the relevant world state to a named slot; the alternative (continuous/streaming persistence with no slots) removes user control over restore points. The choice determines load complexity, corruption behaviour and what design can promise the player.

implementation_variants.name: Named slot with a self-contained serialised snapshot
implementation_variants.description: The standard model: write a complete serialisation of persistable state to a named file (Godot's documented example uses user://savegame.save with FileAccess), and load by reading the whole file back and rebuilding the world.

implementation_variants.name: Slot as a versioned SaveGame object
implementation_variants.description: Unreal's model: a SaveGame object holds the serialised properties and is written to a slot; slot names are the user-facing restore points and the format must be versioned to survive content changes.

implementation_variants.name: Path-independent save/load entry points
implementation_variants.description: Godot's example notes the save and load functions are path independent and can be called from anywhere in the tree, i.e. snapshotting is a global operation over a persist-group rather than a per-object concern.

implementation_variants.name: Staged rebuild on load (reconstruct hierarchy before linking)
implementation_variants.description: Load must reconstruct the object graph in dependency order; Godot documents saving/loading nested persistent objects in stages because NodePaths are otherwise invalid - a direct statement of the load-order problem every snapshot system has.

snapshot_slot_saves.applicability_conditions: Appropriate when the player expects discrete restore points (most single-player campaigns), when the total persistable state is bounded, and when the design wants the player to be able to go back. Less appropriate for persistent shared worlds or games with continuous progression where a slot concept would confuse.
snapshot_slot_saves.limitations: A full snapshot rewrites everything even when little changed, so save size and duration scale with world size. Load must rebuild the entire world, so load times scale the same way, and streaming worlds need special handling. Saves break when the content they reference changes unless versioned and migrated. Slot management (overwrite, delete, cloud conflicts, platform-specific save limits) is user-facing work that is easy to underestimate.
snapshot_slot_saves.required_data_and_tools: A serialisation format with versioning and migration; a persistence grouping (which objects are persisted); a slot manager (create/overwrite/delete/list); platform save-location handling; a migration test suite that loads saves from previous builds; a corrupted-save test.

impact.cpu: medium burst on save and on load (serialise/deserialise plus world rebuild)
impact.gpu: none
impact.ram: medium transient during serialise/deserialise
impact.disk: medium-high: one file per slot, sized by total persistable state
impact.network: none for local slots; cloud-synced slots add upload, conflict and quota handling

snapshot_slot_saves.quality_impact: Determines the player's trust in the game. Losing progress or being unable to load is a severe, memorable failure. Well-implemented slots with clear UI are invisible infrastructure.
snapshot_slot_saves.concept_impact: Enables or forbids design patterns: save-scumming, branching restore points, ironman modes, and any 'revert to before the bad decision' design. Decide the slot policy with design, not after.

effort_person_days.formula: p50 = 2 (persistence grouping + serialisation of one content area) + 2 (slot manager: create/overwrite/delete/list) + 2 (load-order reconstruction) + 1 (versioning + migration path) + 1 (corrupted/old-save tests) = 8; p80 = p50 x ~2.25 (migration of old saves across content changes and platform save-location handling dominate) = 18. Excludes cloud sync and UI polish.

dependencies: A serialisation format with versioning
An agreed definition of what state is persistent
Platform save-location handling

relations.note: Incremental/async writing is an optimisation of the same snapshot data - the slot model defines what, async defines how.
Reconstructing a component-graph entity world on load is the hardest part of snapshot saves; the entity model must be designed for it.
Both are load/rebuild-from-data problems where order and consistency dominate the difficulty.
Both are 'what do we persist/recompute and how much' budget decisions about entity state.

snapshot_slot_saves.verification: Round-trip test: save, quit, reload, and assert a scripted set of world-state assertions match the pre-save state exactly. Then migration test: load a save produced by the previous shipped build and assert it either loads correctly or fails with a clear message (never silently half-loads). Then corruption test: truncate and bit-flip the save file and assert graceful failure with a recoverable state. Finally measure save and load duration against a budget on the slowest target storage.

raycast_vehicle_physics.problem: Simulating a vehicle with full rigid-body suspension and tire models is expensive, unstable and hard to tune. The raycast (or 'spring-on-a-ray') vehicle model replaces the wheel with a downward ray and a spring force, which is cheap, stable, and good enough for arcade and most sim-arcade handling.

implementation_variants.name: Raycast vehicle system with per-wheel spring (Godot VehicleBody3D / VehicleWheel3D)
implementation_variants.description: Godot's VehicleBody3D is explicitly 'based on the raycast vehicle system commonly found in physics engines', requires a VehicleWheel3D node per wheel, and is driven by brake, engine_force and steering; the origin point of the body determines the center of gravity.

implementation_variants.name: Engine-provided lightweight vehicle system (Unreal Chaos Vehicles)
implementation_variants.description: Unreal describes Chaos Vehicles as 'Unreal Engine's lightweight system for performing vehicle physics simulations', and documents a separate guide for building a double-wishbone suspension vehicle and a vehicle center-of-mass page - i.e. the engine exposes both the simple model and a more physical one.

implementation_variants.name: Soft-body node-beam simulation (BeamNG.drive)
implementation_variants.description: The opposite pole: BeamNG documents a soft-body physics approach where the vehicle is simulated as a node-and-beam structure with named beam parameter pairs (e.g. suspension springs, structural beams, steering rack), i.e. the vehicle itself deforms.

implementation_variants.name: Explicitly documented as not realistic - write your own if you need more
implementation_variants.description: Godot states plainly: 'This class has known issues and isn't designed to provide realistic 3D vehicle physics. If you want advanced vehicle physics, you may have to write your own physics integration using CharacterBody3D or RigidBody3D.' This is a published scope limit, not a bug.

raycast_vehicle_physics.applicability_conditions: Arcade, sim-arcade and most action-game vehicles; any game where the vehicle is one of many systems rather than the whole product. Requires a fixed physics timestep for consistent feel. Not appropriate when vehicle deformation or true suspension geometry is a selling point.
raycast_vehicle_physics.limitations: A raycast wheel has no rotational inertia or tire slip model of its own unless added, so tyre-model fidelity is limited. It tunnels at high speed through thin geometry (the ray can miss between steps) unless CCD or multiple rays are used. Godot explicitly states its implementation has known issues and is not designed for realistic vehicle physics. Suspension behaviour is configured on the wheel nodes, not the body, which surprises people. Centre of mass is the body origin, so art and physics origins must be aligned deliberately.
raycast_vehicle_physics.required_data_and_tools: A physics engine with a raycast vehicle model (or a custom one); a fixed physics timestep; a tuning rig for engine force, brake, steering, suspension and centre of mass; a handling test track (straight-line acceleration, braking distance, skidpad, kerb/obstacle test); a high-speed tunnelling test.

impact.cpu: low (a handful of raycasts and spring forces per vehicle per tick) - dramatically cheaper than a full multi-body suspension
impact.gpu: none
impact.ram: negligible per vehicle
impact.network: medium: vehicle physics is highly visible and must be replicated or server-authoritative; Chaos Vehicles explicitly documents async physics support to improve determinism

raycast_vehicle_physics.quality_impact: Decides how driving feels. Raycast vehicles can feel excellent in arcade and sim-arcade games, and the failure mode (floaty, unpredictable, tunnelling) is immediately felt by players.
raycast_vehicle_physics.concept_impact: Determines whether vehicles can be a supporting system in a broad game, or require the whole game to be built around their physics budget and simulation fidelity.

effort_person_days.formula: p50 = 2 (vehicle body + wheel setup) + 3 (handling tuning: engine force, brake, steering, centre of mass) + 3 (suspension tuning and per-wheel configuration) + 2 (anti-tunnelling and high-speed stability) + 2 (handling test track + regression checks) = 12; p80 = p50 x ~2.3 (handling tuning is open-ended and iteration-driven; it is the dominant cost) = 28. Excludes a custom tyre model or soft-body simulation (add 30+).

relations.note: Suspension feel and stability are timestep-dependent; without a fixed step, handling changes with framerate.
A cheap raycast model is what makes it affordable to run many vehicles and to simulate distant ones at reduced fidelity.
Unreal documents async physics support for Chaos Vehicles specifically to improve determinism, which matters for replicated vehicles.
Vehicle raycasts should test only drivable surfaces; layer filtering is the cheapest way to guarantee that.

raycast_vehicle_physics.verification: Run a standardised handling suite and record numeric outputs: 0-to-X acceleration time, braking distance from a given speed, skidpad lateral g, and behaviour over a kerb and a pothole. Assert these are unchanged when the frame rate is varied (proving timestep independence). Then run a high-speed pass over thin geometry and assert no tunnelling. Finally, if vehicles are networked, assert determinism by replaying the same inputs twice and comparing trajectories.

Godot requires a VehicleWheel3D node for each wheel in addition to a CollisionShape3D for the body, and advises that the vehicle's 3D model should generally not include meshes for the wheels.

Godot states: 'This class has known issues and isn't designed to provide realistic 3D vehicle physics. If you want advanced vehicle physics, you may have to write your own physics integration using CharacterBody3D or RigidBody3D.'
Godot states that the origin point of the VehicleBody3D determines the centre of gravity of the vehicle, and that it is usually kept low to make the vehicle more grounded.

In Godot's raycast vehicle, brake only slows the vehicle 'if the wheels are in contact with a surface', and engine_force only accelerates it if wheels with use_as_traction true are in contact with a surface - i.e. all forces are mediated by the wheel raycasts.

vehicle_simulation_lod.problem: A full vehicle simulation is too expensive to run for every vehicle in the world. LOD for vehicle physics means reducing or disabling the simulation for vehicles that are distant, offscreen, player-unowned, or otherwise insignificant - and doing so without the player noticing a behaviour change.

implementation_variants.name: Significance-driven degradation of simulation rate
implementation_variants.description: Use a significance framework to decide which vehicles get a full-rate simulation and which get a reduced rate or a kinematic approximation; Unreal's Significance Manager is documented as the framework for exactly this class of decision, and explicitly does not itself improve performance.

implementation_variants.name: Sleep / deactivation for parked and distant vehicles
implementation_variants.description: Reuse the general physics deactivation mechanism: a vehicle at rest should not be simulated. Godot documents the general per-body sleep mechanism with wake on collision or explicit force/impulse, which is the cheapest form of vehicle LOD.

implementation_variants.name: Model swap: full simulation near, simplified model / kinematic spline far
implementation_variants.description: Replace the physical model with a cheap kinematic or spline-following representation beyond a distance threshold. The specific thresholds and the handover logic are project parameters and are expert_estimate here; no verified primary source documents a shipped swap for vehicles specifically.

implementation_variants.name: Choose the cheaper vehicle model globally (Chaos Vehicles 'lightweight')
implementation_variants.description: The bluntest LOD: pick a vehicle system that is cheap enough to run for everything. Unreal describes Chaos Vehicles as its 'lightweight system for performing vehicle physics simulations'.

vehicle_simulation_lod.applicability_conditions: Any game with more than a few simultaneous vehicles: racing grids, open-world traffic, vehicular combat. Necessary when vehicle count is a design goal. Less relevant when there is one player vehicle and everything else is scripted.
vehicle_simulation_lod.limitations: The handover between simulation levels is where this fails: a vehicle that switches model in view will visibly change behaviour (jerk, different suspension, different collision). Networked vehicles complicate LOD because the server may need to simulate what the client has degraded. Traffic AI that depends on physics state behaves differently at different LODs, so behaviour is not LOD-invariant unless designed to be.
vehicle_simulation_lod.required_data_and_tools: A significance/distance evaluation framework; a physics deactivation mechanism; instrumentation counting fully-simulated vs degraded vehicles; a test scenario where a vehicle crosses the LOD boundary in view; a networking policy for which side simulates.

impact.cpu: high leverage: cost scales with fully-simulated vehicle count rather than total vehicle count
impact.gpu: none (vehicles still render; rendering LOD is a separate system)
impact.ram: low (LOD state per vehicle)
impact.network: risk: LOD decisions made on one machine and not another cause divergence; the simulation authority must be defined

vehicle_simulation_lod.quality_impact: Invisible when the thresholds are right. Visible and bad when they are wrong: distant traffic that slides, or a vehicle that visibly changes handling as it approaches.
vehicle_simulation_lod.concept_impact: Determines how dense traffic can be, which is often the difference between a city that feels alive and one that feels empty.

effort_person_days.formula: p50 = 2 (significance/distance evaluation for vehicles) + 2 (deactivation policy for parked/distant vehicles) + 3 (model or rate swap + handover smoothing) + 2 (instrumentation: full vs degraded counts, CPU cost per tier) + 1 (in-view handover test) = 10; p80 = p50 x ~2.4 (handover artefacts and behaviour divergence between tiers dominate) = 24.

A significance/distance evaluation framework
A defined simulation authority for networked vehicles

relations.note: A cheap raycast model is what makes it possible to keep more vehicles at full simulation rate.
Vehicle LOD reuses the general deactivation mechanism; without it, distant vehicles keep costing.
Same policy shape: evaluate significance, allocate a budget of fully-simulated entities, degrade the rest.
Rendering LOD (impostors) and simulation LOD usually share the same distance thresholds and should be tuned together.

vehicle_simulation_lod.verification: Measure CPU cost per vehicle per simulation tier and assert total vehicle cost is bounded by design as vehicle count grows. Then drive a camera so that a vehicle crosses each LOD boundary in full view and assert no visible positional or rotational discontinuity. Finally, in a multiplayer test, assert that the simulation authority is unambiguous (exactly one machine simulates each vehicle at each moment) and that trajectories do not diverge between tiers in a way the player can see.

Unreal describes Chaos Vehicles as its 'lightweight system for performing vehicle physics simulations', i.e. the engine's own answer to running vehicles cheaply enough that aggressive LOD may be less necessary.

gerstner_fft_water.problem: Realistic open-water surfaces need a wave spectrum rather than a scrolling normal map: summed Gerstner (trochoidal) waves give the characteristic sharp crests, while FFT/Tessendorf spectrum synthesis gives a statistically plausible ocean. Both are more expensive than a scrolling normal map and need care with tiling, LOD and normals.

implementation_variants.name: Summed Gerstner / trochoidal waves
implementation_variants.description: Gerstner (trochoidal) waves are the standard analytic wave form for real-time water: particles move in circular orbits so crests sharpen, unlike a pure sinusoid. Sourced here from an explicitly SECONDARY encyclopedic reference because no primary graphics text was verified in this pass.

implementation_variants.name: FFT / Tessendorf spectrum displacement map, evaluated on the GPU
implementation_variants.description: Doom Eternal's documented water pipeline generates a displacement map and normal map for the water surface 'according to Simulating Ocean Water [Tessendorf2001]', i.e. a spectrum-based (FFT) displacement evaluated off the water plane rather than hand-tuned sine sums.

implementation_variants.name: Projected screen-space grid displaced in world space
implementation_variants.description: Doom Eternal projects a screen-space grid onto the water planes [Johanson2004 projected grid concept], displaces the grid vertices in world space and rasterises the grid - the standard way to get uniform screen-space detail without a huge world-space mesh.

implementation_variants.name: Engine water system with a waves asset (Unreal Water)
implementation_variants.description: Unreal's Water system ships a Water Waves Asset for driving wave simulation and a Single Layer Water shading model, i.e. spectrum-quality water is available as an engine feature rather than a custom shader.

implementation_variants.name: Open-source reference implementation (Crest Ocean System)
implementation_variants.description: Crest is an open-source ocean renderer for Unity that implements LOD'd ocean rendering; cited here as a working reference implementation. Only the repository was verified; no performance figure was retrieved from it.

gerstner_fft_water.applicability_conditions: Open water that is a focal point: ocean gameplay, sailing, coastal set-pieces. Requires the water to be viewed from a constrained camera range (near the surface) where wave shape is legible. Not worth it for incidental water (puddles, small ponds, background rivers) where a scrolling normal map suffices.
gerstner_fft_water.limitations: Spectrum synthesis is bandwidth- and ALU-heavy (texture reads for the displacement map, and for FFT variants multiple passes). Gerstner sums tile visibly if too few waves are used and alias at distance without LOD. Normals derived from displacement are only as good as the sampling; Doom's pipeline renders its water G-buffer and lighting at half horizontal resolution to pay for it. Water interaction with gameplay (buoyancy, boat wakes) is a separate system - Unreal documents a separate buoyancy component and Doom documents a separate height-field hit simulation.
gerstner_fft_water.required_data_and_tools: A spectrum/evaluation shader (custom or engine-provided); a LOD'd water mesh (projected grid or cascaded grid); a normal/displacement generation pass; a water shading model; a profiler separating water passes; a camera-constrained test scene (at surface level, from a distance, and at grazing angles).

impact.cpu: low-medium (grid/mesh generation and parameter updates; mostly GPU-bound otherwise)
impact.gpu: medium-high (displacement generation, world-space vertex displacement, and a dedicated water G-buffer; Doom renders its water G-buffer, SSR and final lighting at half horizontal resolution, which is itself evidence of the cost)
impact.ram: low (wave parameters; simulation grids if interactive)
impact.vram: medium (displacement/normal maps, water G-buffer and half-res targets)
impact.disk: low (no baked assets needed if procedural)
impact.network: none; water is visual and client-local unless gameplay depends on it

gerstner_fft_water.quality_impact: High: this is the difference between water that reads as water and water that reads as a blue plane with a scrolling texture. Most visible at the horizon and at the waterline.
gerstner_fft_water.concept_impact: Enables ocean/sailing/coastal games and water-adjacent set-pieces. Does not itself enable gameplay interaction - that is buoyancy, wakes and flow, each separate.

effort_person_days.formula: p50 = 3 (spectrum/displacement generation pass) + 3 (LOD'd water mesh: projected grid or cascaded grid) + 3 (shading: normals, fresnel, depth-based colour, foam) + 3 (perf: half-res targets, pass merging, overdraw triage) + 2 (horizon and grazing-angle QA) = 14; p80 = p50 x ~2.15 (horizon aliasing, LOD seams and platform-specific degradation dominate) = 30. Much lower if using an engine water system (subtract ~8).

dependencies: A LOD'd water mesh strategy
A dedicated GPU budget for water passes
A separate system for gameplay interaction (buoyancy, wakes)

relations.note: Cheap screen-space/normal-map water is the fallback when the GPU budget cannot accommodate a spectrum water pipeline.
Water is the main consumer of reflection budget; the two must be budgeted together.
Both are 'bake an expensive simulation into a texture' strategies, used for water displacement and for VFX respectively.
Both push work onto the GPU and both end up bounded by bandwidth/overdraw rather than by raw ALU.

gerstner_fft_water.verification: Profile the water passes in isolation (toggle the water system) at the worst camera position - typically at the waterline looking to the horizon - and assert the total fits the allocated budget on the lowest target platform. Then sweep camera height and pitch to check for horizon aliasing and LOD popping. Finally, verify determinism of appearance across frame rates (wave phase should advance with simulation time, not frame count).

claims.statement: Doom Eternal's documented water pipeline generates a displacement map and a normal map for the water surface 'according to Simulating Ocean Water [Tessendorf2001]', i.e. a 2001 spectrum-synthesis (FFT) reference rather than hand-tuned wave sums.
claims.locator: PDF p.58, 'DISPLACEMENT MAP' slide and reference list

claims.statement: Doom Eternal projects a screen-space grid onto the water planes (citing Johanson 2004, 'Real-Time Water Rendering - Introducing the Projected Grid Concept'), displaces grid vertices in world space, and renders the water by rasterising that grid.
Doom Eternal renders the water planes depth image at the same resolution as the screen-space grid, 256x256.
claims.locator: PDF p.60, 'GENERATE WATER SURFACE MESH' - 'Depth image (256x256)'

claims.statement: Doom Eternal renders its water G-buffer, its water-surface SSR and its final water lighting at 1/2 horizontal resolution - a concrete, published example of water pass budgeting in a shipped game.
claims.locator: PDF p.63 ('G-Buffer (1/2 horizontal resolution)'), p.67 ('Water SSR (1/2 horizontal resolution)'), p.68 ('Water final (1/2 horizontal resolution)')

claims.statement: Doom Eternal simulates water hits as a separate height-field simulation [Müller-Fischer2008] on a single 512x512 grid centred on the camera with top-down projection, snapped to grid-cell multiples to avoid reprojection aliasing, and adds the resulting heightfield as extra displacement to the water vertices.

Doom Eternal rasterises flowing water surfaces directly to the water G-buffer with normals perturbed by artist-authored normal and flow maps, and applies no displacement to flowing surfaces - which the presenters themselves flag as 'room for improvement'.
claims.locator: PDF p.76, 'ADDING SUPPORT FOR FLOWING WATER'

claims.statement: The Gerstner/trochoidal wave description is cited from an encyclopedic (SECONDARY) source, not from a primary graphics text or a vendor SDK, because no primary Gerstner reference was verified in this pass. Treat it as background, not as evidence of a specific implementation.
Unreal's Water system documents a Water Waves Asset for driving wave simulation and a Single Layer Water shading model, i.e. spectrum-driven water is available as a shipped engine feature.
claims.locator: 'Essentials' links: 'Simulating Waves Using The Water Waves Asset', 'Single Layer Water Shading Model'

game_examples.fact: The shipped water pipeline generates a Tessendorf-style displacement and normal map, projects a screen-space grid onto water planes and displaces vertices in world space, and renders the water G-buffer, water SSR and final water lighting at 1/2 horizontal resolution; interactive water hits use a single 512x512 height field centred on the camera.
game_examples.non_transferable: These are concrete published pipeline parameters for that game on its target hardware. The half-resolution choice and the 512x512 grid are design decisions with visible quality consequences that another project must re-justify; they are not recommended defaults. No frame-time figure is claimed for water from this source.

planar_reflection_budget.problem: Water and other reflective surfaces need a reflection source. A planar reflection re-renders the scene from a mirrored camera into a render target - accurate but a second scene render. A reflection budget decides resolution, update rate and object filtering, and is usually the difference between affordable and unaffordable water.

implementation_variants.name: Screen-space reflection at reduced resolution (Doom Eternal)
implementation_variants.description: Rather than a full planar re-render, Doom Eternal computes water-surface SSR into an SSR image using depth and normals from its G-buffer, at 1/2 horizontal resolution - i.e. the reflection is a screen-space pass at reduced resolution, budgeted like any other pass.

implementation_variants.name: Split before/after-water buffers to composite refraction and reflection
implementation_variants.description: Doom Eternal splits the main colour buffer into before-water and after-water pixels before rendering transparent surfaces, renders transparents into those buffers by comparing fragment depth against the water G-buffer depth, and needs an extra target to track before-water alpha - a concrete published example of paying for water compositing with extra render targets rather than with a full re-render.

implementation_variants.name: Engine-provided water reflection/shading path
implementation_variants.description: Unreal's Water system documents a Single Layer Water shading model and a water scalability/debugging page, i.e. reflection quality is exposed as a scalable setting rather than being hard-coded.

implementation_variants.name: Explicit resolution/update-rate budget (the general shape)
implementation_variants.description: The general policy - render the reflection at a fraction of screen resolution, update at a fraction of frame rate, and exclude object classes - is standard practice. No primary source stating universal parameters was verified; this variant is expert_estimate.

planar_reflection_budget.applicability_conditions: Any water or mirror surface where the reflection carries information the player reads. Budgeting is mandatory once there is more than one reflective surface, or once the scene is fill-rate bound. Screen-space approaches require a G-buffer with depth and normals and fail for off-screen geometry.
planar_reflection_budget.limitations: Screen-space reflections cannot show geometry that is off-screen or behind the reflector, producing missing or clipped reflections at screen edges - the reason a planar pass is sometimes still needed. Reduced-resolution reflections alias and shimmer with TAA. A planar reflection is a full second scene render: it roughly doubles geometry and draw cost for the reflected view unless aggressively filtered. Update-rate reduction causes visible lag in the reflection during fast motion.
planar_reflection_budget.required_data_and_tools: A render-target manager with resolution scaling; a per-pass GPU timer; a filtered object list for the reflection pass; a TAA/upsampling path for reduced-resolution targets; a test scene with fast camera motion over water and with off-screen geometry that should be visible in the reflection.

impact.cpu: medium if a planar pass is used (a second visibility/cull/draw submission set); low for screen-space only
impact.gpu: high for a full-resolution planar pass; reduced materially by half/quarter resolution and by update-rate reduction - Doom Eternal's choice of 1/2 horizontal resolution for water SSR is a published instance
impact.ram: low
impact.vram: medium-high (reflection render targets; Doom's approach adds dedicated before/after-water targets plus an alpha target)
impact.network: none

planar_reflection_budget.quality_impact: Reflections are a large part of whether water reads as water. Under-budgeted, they produce shimmer and missing geometry; over-budgeted, they cost the frame.
planar_reflection_budget.concept_impact: Determines whether waterfront/mirror-heavy environments are viable, and therefore affects level and art direction.

effort_person_days.formula: p50 = 2 (render target + resolution scaling) + 2 (object filtering for the reflection pass) + 2 (update-rate reduction + upsample/TAA) + 2 (per-pass GPU timing and budget allocation) + 2 (QA: fast motion, screen edges, off-screen geometry) = 10; p80 = p50 x ~2.2 (edge artefacts and TAA shimmer on reduced-resolution targets dominate) = 22.

dependencies: A G-buffer with depth and normals (for screen-space approaches)
A render-target manager with resolution scaling
An allocated GPU budget for reflection passes

relations.note: Water shading and water reflection are the same budget line in practice; Doom Eternal budgets them together at half horizontal resolution.
Screen-space water and screen-space reflections share the same failure mode (missing off-screen information) and the same mitigation.
Both are 'render a cheaper version of the scene into a buffer' techniques with resolution and update-rate budgets.
Transparent particles and reflections interact badly: Doom Eternal needs a dedicated before-water alpha target precisely because of this.

planar_reflection_budget.verification: Enable per-pass GPU timing and record the cost of the reflection pass at full, half and quarter resolution with and without update-rate reduction, then pick the setting that fits the budget. Then move the camera fast over the water and assert the reflection does not visibly lag or shimmer (or that the shimmer is acceptable with TAA). Finally, place geometry that is visible in the reflection but off-screen in the main view and document whether the chosen approach can show it - if it cannot, confirm the art direction tolerates that.

claims.statement: Doom Eternal computes water-surface SSR into an SSR image using depth and normals from the G-buffer at 1/2 horizontal resolution.
claims.locator: PDF p.67, 'WATER SURFACE SSR' - 'Water SSR (1/2 horizontal resolution)'

claims.statement: Doom Eternal splits the main colour buffer into before-water and after-water pixels before rendering transparent surfaces, compares fragment depth against water G-buffer depth, and needs an additional target to track before-water alpha - i.e. water compositing is paid for with extra render targets.
claims.locator: PDF p.69-p.71, 'PREPARATION BEFORE RENDERING TRANSPARENT SURFACES' / 'RENDER TRANSPARENT SURFACES'

claims.statement: Doom Eternal's final water composite uses a distorted texcoord lookup [Sousa2008] for the after-water image, i.e. refraction is a screen-space distortion at composite time.
Unreal's Water system documents water debugging and scalability options as a first-class page, i.e. water/reflection quality is expected to be scaled per platform rather than fixed.

No verified primary source was found that publishes the cost of a true planar (mirrored-camera) reflection pass in a shipped game. The claim that a planar reflection is roughly a second scene render is derived from what the technique requires, not from a cited measurement; treat it as a directional statement.
claims.locator: no planar reflection cost figures found in verified sources

claims.statement: Screen-space reflection uses depth and normals from the G-buffer, so it can only reflect what is already on screen - geometry outside the main view cannot appear in the reflection. This is a structural limitation of the technique, not a tuning problem.
claims.locator: PDF p.67, method description ('using depth and normals from G-buffer')

game_examples.fact: Water reflection is screen-space SSR computed at 1/2 horizontal resolution from the G-buffer, composited via split before/after-water buffers with a distorted texcoord lookup, and paid for with extra render targets rather than a full planar re-render.
game_examples.non_transferable: This is one shipped game's published solution on its target hardware. The half-resolution choice is a trade with visible consequences (softer, aliasing-prone reflections) that another project must re-evaluate; no millisecond cost for the reflection pass is published and nothing transfers as a budget.

screen_space_water_simple.problem: Full spectrum/FFT water is often too expensive for the water's actual screen importance - incidental rivers, puddles, small ponds, or water on a lower-end platform. A screen-space or cheap-approximation water surface (normal-map scrolling, projected grid with minimal displacement, small height-field simulation, no reflection pass) delivers acceptable water at a fraction of the cost.

implementation_variants.name: Artist-authored flow/normal maps with no displacement (Doom Eternal flowing water)
implementation_variants.description: Doom Eternal rasterises flowing water surfaces directly to the water G-buffer, perturbing normals with artist-authored normal and flow maps and applying no displacement at all - the presenters flag the lack of displacement as 'room for improvement', which is exactly the trade this method makes deliberately.

implementation_variants.name: Small camera-centred height-field simulation for interaction
implementation_variants.description: When the water must react (footsteps, impacts), Doom Eternal uses one 512x512 height-field grid centred on the camera with top-down projection, snapped to grid-cell multiples to avoid reprojection aliasing, reprojected when the camera moves - a bounded, camera-local simulation rather than a world-wide one.

implementation_variants.name: Caustics generated from the displacement map and reused next frame
implementation_variants.description: Doom Eternal generates a caustics image from the water displacement map by rasterising a grid mesh aligned to it and perturbing each vertex by simulated refraction to a constant depth, then projects the resulting image onto underwater/scene geometry the next frame - a one-frame-delayed cheap approximation rather than a real caustic solve.

implementation_variants.name: Engine single-layer water shading with scalable settings
implementation_variants.description: Unreal documents a Single Layer Water shading model and water scalability options, i.e. a cheap, scalable water path is a shipped engine feature that can be selected instead of the full water pipeline.

screen_space_water_simple.applicability_conditions: Incidental or background water; low-end or last-generation platforms; games where water is set dressing rather than a focal point. Also appropriate as the LOD fallback for a game that has expensive water near the player and cheap water in the distance.
screen_space_water_simple.limitations: Screen-space and normal-map water has no real geometry at the waterline, so shorelines and object intersections read as flat or wrong. It cannot show reflections of off-screen geometry. It does not support real buoyancy, waves that affect gameplay, or convincing underwater views. A camera-local height field only simulates interaction near the camera, so distant interactions are simply absent.
screen_space_water_simple.required_data_and_tools: A water shading model with normal/flow map support; optionally a small render-target height field for interaction; a depth-based colour/fresnel/foam term; a waterline/shore blending solution (this is where most of the art effort goes); a per-pass GPU timer to confirm the saving versus the full path.

impact.cpu: low (little or no simulation; mostly parameter updates)
impact.gpu: low-medium (a transparent shaded surface plus optional small render targets) - materially cheaper than the spectrum pipeline it replaces
impact.ram: low
impact.vram: low-medium (normal/flow maps and small render targets)
impact.network: none

screen_space_water_simple.quality_impact: Acceptable at a distance and in passing; reads as flat or fake at the waterline and in close-ups. The waterline/shoreline blend is what determines whether it is acceptable or obviously cheap.
screen_space_water_simple.concept_impact: Lets water appear in environments and on platforms where the full pipeline would have forced it to be cut - preserving art direction at lower cost.

effort_person_days.formula: p50 = 2 (water shading model: normals, flow, fresnel, depth colour) + 2 (waterline/shoreline blending - the hard part) + 1 (optional small height-field interaction) + 1 (scalability settings for lower platforms) + 1 (pass-cost comparison vs the full path) = 7; p80 = p50 x ~2.3 (shoreline and intersection artefacts dominate the iteration) = 16. Subtract ~3 if using an engine single-layer water model.

dependencies: A transparent water shading model
A solution for the waterline where water meets geometry
A GPU budget comparison against the full water path

relations.note: The cheap path is the fallback when spectrum water is unaffordable; many projects ship both and select by distance/importance.
Cheap water usually means dropping or heavily reducing the reflection pass, which is where most of the saving comes from.
Both replace a real simulation with a cheap, camera-facing approximation that holds up only under constrained viewing conditions.
Same philosophy: a cheap proxy selected by distance/importance, judged entirely by whether the transition is noticeable.

screen_space_water_simple.verification: Measure the GPU cost of the simple path and the full path in the same view and record the delta - this is the entire justification for the method and must be a measurement, not an assumption. Then inspect the waterline from a low camera and from a distance and assert the shoreline blend is acceptable. Finally, if interaction is included, verify that interactions outside the simulated region are either absent by design or hidden.

claims.statement: Doom Eternal rasterises flowing water surfaces directly to the water G-buffer, perturbs normals with artist-authored normal and flow maps, and applies no displacement to flowing surfaces - flagged in the presentation itself as room for improvement.
claims.locator: PDF p.76, 'ADDING SUPPORT FOR FLOWING WATER'

claims.statement: Doom Eternal simulates water hits on one 512x512 grid centred on the camera with top-down projection, reprojects the previous frame's height field as the camera moves, and snaps the grid position to a multiple of the cell size to avoid reprojection aliasing.

Doom Eternal generates caustics from the water displacement map by rasterising an aligned grid mesh and perturbing each vertex by simulated refraction to a constant depth; the resulting caustics image is used the next frame, projected onto geometry that is underwater or just above water.
Unreal documents a Single Layer Water shading model and a water debugging/scalability page, i.e. a cheaper water shading path with platform scalability is a shipped engine feature.
claims.locator: 'Essentials' links: 'Single Layer Water Shading Model', 'Water Debugging and Scalability Options'

claims.statement: Unreal documents water buoyancy as a separate component from the water rendering/meshing system, i.e. gameplay interaction with water is not included in a cheap screen-space water surface and must be added separately.

No published millisecond comparison of a cheap screen-space water path against a full spectrum water path was found in the verified sources; Doom Eternal documents the cheap techniques but not their measured saving versus the expensive path.
claims.locator: water section - techniques documented, no comparative measurements

game_examples.fact: The shipped game uses deliberately cheap approximations for non-hero water: flowing water with no displacement at all, a single 512x512 camera-centred height field for interaction, and caustics generated from the displacement map and reused one frame later.
game_examples.locator: PDF p.72 ('WATER HITS SIMULATION'), p.74 ('WATER CAUSTICS'), p.76 ('ADDING SUPPORT FOR FLOWING WATER')
game_examples.non_transferable: These are documented simplifications in one shipped game, chosen against its own art direction and hardware. The absence of displacement on flowing water is explicitly noted as a known compromise; another project may not be able to accept it. No cost figure for these approximations is published.
